These readings say nothing reliable about illness on their own: symptoms go to a doctor, and anything that feels like a heart rhythm problem goes there promptly.

practices.title: The six-area check
practices.summary: Roughly monthly, twenty minutes naming which of six things is actually wrong — workload, control, reward, community, fairness or values — and who you will say it to out loud.
practices.why: Burnout research has been fairly steady for three decades about where the problem sits: a sustained mismatch between a person and their job, most often too much work with too little say over how it is done. That conclusion is awkward for wellbeing apps and worth stating plainly — reviews of workplace trials find that changing the work outperforms training the individual, and the individual programmes that do help tend to produce small effects that fade. Naming the specific mismatch turns a vague sense of being fried into something a manager, a peer or a professional can act on.
practices.safety: A structural review, not a resilience exercise, and the limit deserves saying plainly: no breathing practice and no evening routine will fix a job with an impossible workload or no control over how the work is done. If the honest answer is that the work itself has to change, the next steps are your manager, your union or professional body, or a different job. And if you are at dread, numbness, or thoughts of not wanting to be here, that is a doctor or therapist today — not a monthly review.

practices.title: The message you nearly didn’t send
practices.summary: Five minutes to message someone you have drifted from — no ask, no plan, just that you thought of them.
practices.why: People are poor judges of this one. Across repeated experiments, senders consistently underestimated how much a small out-of-the-blue check-in mattered to the person on the other end, and the gap was widest exactly where contact had lapsed and the message came as a surprise. "They probably don’t want to hear from me" is the belief the evidence argues with, which is why this aims at the belief rather than at your calendar.
practices.safety: Send it and let it go — a slow reply, or none, is usually a busy week rather than a verdict. Where someone has asked for space, respect that instead.

practices.title: Answer the good news properly
practices.summary: Ten minutes to go back to the good news a friend shared and reply like you mean it: ask for the detail, say why it lands.
practices.why: How you answer someone’s good news appears to matter as much as how you answer their bad news. Diary and lab work links warm, curious replies with both people feeling closer afterwards, while a flat acknowledgement reads as indifference even when none was meant. Most of this research was done inside couples and measures how people already respond more often than it changes it, so the direction is reasonably solid and the size is not.
practices.safety: Their good news, on their terms — this is about answering well, not about producing enthusiasm you do not feel. Reaching out is the part you control and the reply is not, so a message that goes nowhere says nothing about you. If loneliness has stopped feeling like something a plan can fix, that is worth raising with a GP — and Lifeline is 13 11 14, any hour.

practices.title: The standing thing
practices.summary: One activity with the same people at the same hour every week, decided once so nobody has to organise it again.
practices.why: Adult friendships mostly form as a by-product of repeated shared time rather than from deciding to be closer, and familiarity does much of the early work. A standing slot removes the weekly negotiation that quietly kills most plans. The count-the-hours research everyone quotes here is a single study on a modest sample using recalled estimates, so we keep the direction — ordinary hours side by side accumulate into closeness — and leave its specific thresholds alone.
practices.safety: A standing plan is meant to take organising off you, not to become another thing to keep up. Miss one and the next one still stands. None of this applies where you are afraid of the person, where you are being controlled, or where money, contact or freedom is being used against you. That is not a communication problem and nothing on this card will help with it. 1800RESPECT is 1800 737 732, free and confidential, twenty-four hours.

practices.title: Belong to something that meets
practices.summary: Turn up to one group that meets whether or not you do — a club, a team, a choir, a regular table.
practices.why: A sizeable body of research on group membership and health finds that the number of groups people genuinely feel part of tracks with steadier mood and better wellbeing through hard stretches, and that losing memberships — a move, a job change, retirement — is often when people come unstuck. Most of it is cohort and longitudinal work, so read belonging as protective company you take part in rather than something the group does to you.
practices.safety: Attendance is the whole practice — a group you dread is the wrong group, not a discipline problem. Swap it rather than defend it.

practices.title: Who you actually miss
practices.summary: Roughly monthly, fifteen written minutes: who you feel close to, who you have drifted from, and one name to move on this month.
practices.why: Being short of company and feeling unknown are different problems with different answers, and a full calendar hides the second one well. Large observational studies link both the countable version and the felt version to worse long-term health — a strong and consistent association, but drawn from watching populations rather than from showing that adding contacts changes the outcome. The written pass itself is our structure: a way to catch the drift while it is still cheap to reverse.
practices.safety: A prompt for noticing, not a scorecard on your friendships. Loneliness that sits heavily for months, or arrives alongside low mood, is worth raising with a doctor rather than writing your way through.

practices.title: Annual capacity benchmark
practices.summary: Once a year, the same three tests on the same morning: a timed hard walk or run, a hang or loaded carry for time, and a one-leg balance hold.
practices.why: Aerobic capacity and grip strength are two of the sharpest predictors of how long people live in very large observational studies — hundreds of thousands of adults followed for years, with the gap between fittest and least fit wider than for most risk factors anyone talks about. Both capacities respond to training, but no one has shown that moving your number moves your lifespan, so read this as a signal about your trajectory rather than a lever you pull.
practices.safety: A hard-effort test is genuinely hard: build to it over weeks, and stop for chest pain, unusual breathlessness or dizziness. Talk to your doctor before testing if you have a heart condition, are pregnant, or have been away from training. A field test only estimates — a real laboratory measurement is something a doctor or exercise physiologist orders and interprets.

practices.title: Floor-to-stand practice
practices.summary: Twice a week: lower yourself to the floor and stand back up five times with as little hand support as you can manage.
practices.why: In a cohort of roughly two thousand adults aged 51 to 80, those who needed more support to get down to the floor and back up were more likely to die in the years that followed. That is one population, scored by eye, and anyone who can do it unaided is probably healthier in a dozen unmeasured ways — so treat the link as a hint rather than a finding to lean on. The practice earns its place regardless: getting off the floor unaided is a large part of what decides whether later decades are lived independently.
practices.safety: Practise next to a wall or a sturdy chair, on a soft surface, hands available — the aim is to need them less over months, not to risk a fall today. Knee, hip or back trouble, or any history of falls, is a conversation with a doctor or physiotherapist before you start.

practices.title: Blood pressure check
practices.summary: One morning a week, before coffee: sit still for five minutes, take two readings a minute apart, and write both down in the same place.
practices.why: Raised blood pressure carries no symptoms until it has already done damage, and one reading taken in a clinic is a poor guide to your real average. Randomised trials find that people who check at home and bring the numbers back to a clinician end up better controlled than people who do not — the checking helps because of the conversation it feeds, not on its own.
practices.safety: You are collecting numbers, not reading them: your doctor is the one who says what your readings mean, what follows from them, and how often you should be checking at all. A very high reading, or one alongside chest pain, a severe headache or changes in vision, is a same-day medical call rather than a data point.

practices.title: The yearly health conversation
practices.summary: Once a year, book the appointment and arrive with a written list: family history, the numbers you have been tracking, and what is worth checking at your age.
practices.why: Reviews of routine annual check-ups have found that the appointment by itself does not lower the odds of dying — an uncomfortable result, and one worth knowing before you build a habit on it. What does hold up is specific, age-appropriate checking of things like blood pressure, cholesterol and blood sugar, and having a clinician who has met you before and can see a trend rather than a snapshot. The value sits in arriving prepared with the right questions.
practices.safety: Which tests belong in your year is a medical judgement resting on your age, history and family — your doctor orders them and your doctor interprets them with you. IntentNorth never says what to test for, what a result means, or what to do next; it only keeps the appointment in your calendar. Educational structure, not medical advice.

practices.title: Daily step floor
practices.summary: Hold a floor of roughly 7,000–8,000 steps a day: glance at the count mid-afternoon and top it up before dinner on the days you are short.
practices.why: Across pooled studies that counted steps with devices rather than questionnaires, adults who walked more had lower death rates over the following years, with most of the separation already banked by about seven or eight thousand a day and little further gain above that. It is observational — people who walk a lot differ from people who do not in many ways at once — but consistent across cohorts. A floor beats a target because it counts everything: the walk to the station, the pacing during calls, the block after lunch.
practices.safety: A floor, not a debt — a missed day is not something to repay with a forced march. Chest pain, calf pain or unusual breathlessness while walking is a reason to see a doctor, not to train harder.

practices.title: One lever at a time
practices.summary: Once a week, ten minutes picking the single food change you will actually run for the next seven days — and then not going looking for a better diet.
practices.why: This is the best-supported finding in weight management, and almost the opposite of what the industry sells. When named diets are put head to head in large randomised trials, the differences between the diets come out small. What separates people is whether they kept doing the thing: in one four-programme trial, self-rated adherence tracked strongly with how much weight came off while the assigned diet did not, and another found a spread of outcomes inside each arm running from a large loss to a modest gain. The useful question is never which diet is best. It is which single change you can still be doing in three months.
practices.safety: One lever, chosen by you, and no target number attached to it — IntentNorth never sets a calorie figure, a weight to reach, or a rate to lose at, because those belong to a doctor or a registered dietitian who knows your history. Skip this and the rest of this group entirely if you have ever had an eating disorder or think you might now: structured food planning is a known trigger. If choosing a lever turns into rules that keep multiplying, stop and talk to your GP or a dietitian rather than trying harder.

practices.title: The weekly trend read
practices.summary: One morning a week, same day, same conditions: step on, write it down, and read only the line across the last month — never the reading itself.
practices.why: Regular self-weighing genuinely holds up, most clearly in maintenance: a randomised trial of people who had already lost a substantial amount put weighing at the centre of a self-regulation programme and saw less regain than a newsletter control. The mechanism is unglamorous — it turns a slow drift into something you can respond to early. But the number itself is mostly noise. Day-to-day movement is water, salt, glycogen and where you are in your cycle, none of which is what you are trying to see. Reading a single morning as a verdict on a week of effort is where this practice stops helping and starts hurting.
practices.safety: This is the protocol in the library most likely to be run compulsively, so read this before starting it. Weighing can slide into weighing several times a day, into deciding what you deserve to eat from what the scale said — and a randomised trial in young women found daily weighing produced more mood swing and lower body satisfaction than a control activity, so the harm is not hypothetical. Once a week is the whole protocol; more often is not more commitment. If you have ever had an eating disorder, do not run this at all — no scale, and a conversation with your GP or a registered dietitian instead. If the weekly reading leaves you more anxious than informed, delete it and lose nothing that matters.

practices.title: A protein anchor at every meal
practices.summary: Build lunch and dinner around a palm-sized piece of protein first, then fill the plate around it.
practices.why: Protein is the one macronutrient where the composition argument earns its keep, and satiety is why. Controlled feeding work shows people eating a higher-protein diet settle at a lower food intake without being asked to hold back, and a meta-analysis of nearly forty randomised trials found higher-protein arms ended around 1.6 kg lighter than controls — real, and also modest. Protein protects lean mass while weight is coming off, which is the part most diets quietly get wrong. Worth knowing the limit: at least one trial found the extra fullness did not translate into eating less later when highly palatable food was around.
practices.safety: An anchor to build around, not a rule to obey, and no food is off the plate because of it. Kidney or liver conditions, pregnancy, and any medical eating plan mean your doctor or dietitian sets your protein intake, not IntentNorth. If ordering your plate by macronutrient starts to feel like a set of rules you can fail, drop the protocol — that shift is the early shape of disordered eating.

practices.title: Slow the plate down
practices.summary: One meal a day eaten slowly — fork down between mouthfuls, no screen, the meal given at least twenty minutes.
practices.why: Eating rate is one of the few things that changes how much you eat without changing what you eat: a meta-analysis of around twenty studies found slower eating led to meaningfully lower intake within the meal. The caveats are large, which is why this is moderate rather than good — almost all of it is single-meal laboratory work, slowing down did not reliably change hunger hours later, and one trial found the effect in normal-weight participants but not in participants with overweight. Nobody has shown that a slower fork changes body weight months later. It is cheap and it makes the meal better on its own terms.
practices.safety: Slowing down is meant to make a meal more enjoyable, not more supervised. If paying attention to how you eat turns into monitoring every mouthful, or into stopping meals early, stop running this one. Anyone with a history of an eating disorder should skip it, and take it to a registered dietitian or GP rather than an app.

practices.title: Switch to maintenance on purpose
practices.summary: Roughly monthly, fifteen minutes deciding whether you are still in a change phase or have moved into holding — and naming which handful of behaviours you are keeping either way.
practices.why: The part that gets no attention is the part that decides the outcome. Systematic reviews find most of what came off tends to come back, and one randomised comparison of fast versus slow loss saw both groups regain around seven-tenths of it. The reason is not weakness — maintenance is a different job from losing, and almost nobody is taught it. It has been tested directly: a structured self-regulation programme produced less regain than newsletters alone. Maintenance needs declaring rather than drifting into, and it needs its own small set of behaviours you intend to keep for years, not the whole apparatus.
practices.safety: Maintenance here means the behaviours you keep and a trend line that sits flat — IntentNorth does not name a weight to hold, a range to stay inside, or a shape to aim at. A flat trend that wobbles is what maintaining looks like; it is not a failed change phase. If the idea of stopping active weight loss feels intolerable, that is worth saying out loud to a GP or registered dietitian, because it is one of the more reliable early signs of disordered eating.

practices.title: Two weeks of photographs
practices.summary: For two weeks only, photograph what you eat — no numbers, no scoring — then look back once and pick the one pattern worth changing.
practices.why: Writing down what you eat is one of the most consistent behavioural correlates of weight change there is, and randomised trials of app-based self-monitoring find a couple of kilograms of difference against no monitoring. Some of that is circular — people doing well log more — but the plausible mechanism is simple: most people have an inaccurate picture of what they eat, and seeing it makes a lever obvious. This is graded moderate because we deliberately changed what was tested: the trials counted calories and this version strips the numbers out, because a running total is the most reliable route from tracking into compulsion. That substitution is our judgement call and has not been tested.
practices.safety: Food logging is the other practice here that runs compulsively, and it does so quietly — two weeks becomes two years, photographs acquire numbers, and a record becomes a scorecard. The two-week limit is the protocol, not a suggestion: stop on the day. No calorie figures, no scoring a day as a success or failure. If you have ever had an eating disorder, or find yourself unable to stop when the fortnight ends, do not run this and take it to your GP or a registered dietitian.

practices.title: Thirty grams of fibre
practices.summary: Build the day toward roughly 30 g of fibre — a fibre-anchored first meal, then beans, lentils, whole grains, fruit, nuts and skins across the rest.
practices.why: This is the strongest thing nutrition has to say that almost nobody acts on. A series of systematic reviews pooled 185 prospective studies alongside 58 controlled trials and found the people eating the most fibre had roughly 15–30% lower rates of dying from any cause, of coronary heart disease, stroke, type 2 diabetes and colorectal cancer than those eating the least, with most of the separation banked between 25 g and 29 g a day. The trials agreed on the mechanisms you can measure in weeks: blood pressure, cholesterol and body weight all moved. The hard outcomes are observational, and high-fibre eaters differ in many ways at once. What makes it worth a protocol is the gap: most adults average around 19 g, and fewer than one in ten reach 30.
practices.safety: Build up over a few weeks rather than in a day, and drink water alongside — a sudden jump is what causes the bloating people then blame fibre for. Gut symptoms that persist are a doctor’s job and not something to eat your way out of: any bleeding, unexplained weight loss, or a change in your bowel habit lasting more than a few weeks is an appointment. If you live with a diagnosed bowel condition, ask your clinician which fibre pattern suits you before changing anything.

practices.title: Water is the default drink
practices.summary: Make water or something unsweetened the automatic answer to thirst, so a sugary drink becomes a thing you choose rather than the thing already in your hand.
practices.why: Sugar-sweetened drinks are the clearest single-food association in nutrition epidemiology, and unusually there are also randomised trials. Giving children a masked sugar-free drink instead of a sugar-containing one, 250 ml a day for 18 months, produced measurably less weight and fat gain; a parallel trial in teenagers found the same over a year, though the gap closed once support stopped. The mechanism is well demonstrated: calories drunk are barely compensated for at the next meal, so they add rather than replace. The cohort evidence carries the usual confounding and the trials are in young people over months — it is still the single highest-yield swap in the pillar.
practices.safety: A change of default, not a ban — the birthday drink is not the problem this addresses. Educational structure, not medical advice: if you live with diabetes or kidney disease, what and how much you drink is part of a medical picture, and your clinician’s guidance comes first.

practices.title: A fermented food a day
practices.summary: One serving of a live fermented food most days — plain yoghurt, kefir, kimchi, sauerkraut, miso — folded into a meal you already eat.
practices.why: One well-run trial sits behind this and it is worth knowing in detail. Researchers randomised 36 healthy adults to either a fermented-food arm or a high-fibre arm for ten weeks. The fermented arm’s gut microbial diversity rose and nineteen inflammatory proteins fell, with larger changes in people eating more servings. The high-fibre arm showed neither on average over that window, which the researchers said plainly had surprised them. Read it carefully: 36 people at one site for ten weeks, working up to around six servings a day, with immune markers rather than illness as the outcome, and nothing of that size has replicated it. It does not argue against fibre, whose evidence is for disease over decades — it suggests the two work on different timescales.
practices.safety: Ordinary foods, nothing bought off a shelf of pills, and no amount to hit. Unpasteurised ferments are not for everyone — in pregnancy, or with a suppressed immune system, ask your doctor which are fine for you. Bloating, pain or a change in bowel habit that persists is a medical question rather than a food-diary one.

practices.title: Planned drink-free days
practices.summary: Name the drink-free days before the week starts — three is a good default — and keep alcohol to the days you chose rather than the days you fancied it.
practices.why: Start with what IntentNorth will not tell you. The comfortable story that a moderate amount protects the heart has been substantially undermined: much of the apparent benefit came from counting people who had stopped drinking because they were already unwell as non-drinkers, and a meta-analysis found that once studies handled those biases, low intake showed no mortality advantage over lifetime abstention. Genetic studies that sidestep lifestyle confounding find no protective signal either. So there is no healthy amount for us to name, and we will not invent one. What is well supported is direction: less is better. The reason to schedule days rather than set a weekly number is behavioural — a rule decided in advance removes a nightly decision that tends to resolve one way.
practices.safety: If cutting down feels hard, if you drink every day, or if stopping brings shakes, sweating, a racing heart or bad anxiety, talk to a doctor before changing anything — stopping abruptly is genuinely unsafe for some people, and effective help exists and works. This is a planning habit for ordinary drinking and nothing more; a scheduling app is the wrong tool for dependence.

practices.title: A glass with every meal
practices.summary: A glass of water with each meal, and one within arm’s reach where you work — no daily litre target, no bottle to tick off.
practices.why: Almost everything popularly said about hydration is folklore, so this protocol is deliberately modest. The eight-glasses rule has no traceable evidence behind it — a physiologist went looking for its origin and could not find one — and surveys show most healthy people drink less than that and are fine. Thirst is a reasonable guide for a healthy adult: it starts once blood concentration has risen by under 2%, while dehydration proper begins around 5%, so being thirsty is an early warning rather than a late one. The confident claims that mild under-drinking wrecks concentration rest on small studies with mixed replication and a design you cannot blind. What survives is unglamorous: attach fluid to moments you already have and keep it in sight.
practices.safety: Thirst stops being a reliable guide in older age, in hot weather, during long or hard exercise, and with some conditions and medicines — those are cases to ask a doctor about rather than guess at. More is not better: drinking large volumes quickly can be dangerous. If a clinician has told you to limit or increase fluids, follow that and ignore this.

practices.title: Vegetables and protein first
practices.summary: At the day’s biggest meal, eat the vegetables and the protein before you start on the rice, bread, pasta or potato.
practices.why: The finding is real but small in every sense. In crossover studies of eleven and then sixteen people with type 2 diabetes, the same meal eaten in a different order produced substantially lower glucose and insulin rises when the starch came last, and the pattern has repeated in prediabetes and in gestational diabetes. That is a reproducible effect measured over hours, in tiny groups, mostly in people already living with a glucose problem — nobody has shown it changes anything over years, and how much survives in a healthy person is unknown. It stays because it is free: it changes no shopping, costs no time, and nudges the vegetables from garnish to first course.
practices.safety: A way of ordering a plate, not a way of managing a condition. If you live with diabetes or take anything that affects blood sugar, your clinician’s plan is the one that counts and nothing here changes it.

practices.title: If-then your three riskiest moments
practices.summary: Once a week, write your three riskiest moments as “when X happens, I do Y” — Y being something you actually do, not something you avoid.
practices.why: Naming the exact cue and the exact response in advance is the best-replicated finding in behaviour change: around ninety-four studies pooled to a medium-to-large effect, working hardest on the intentions people keep failing to act on, because the decision is already made before the moment arrives. Two details carry the weight. The plan must name a real situation — the fourth round at the same table, the phone at 11pm — not a vague day. And the “then” must be an action you perform rather than one you withhold: plans written as “I will not” leave you nothing to do with the moment. This is also why willpower is the wrong frame: the claim that self-control is a fuel tank that empties has failed large multi-lab replication, so any plan whose active ingredient is wanting it more is not a plan.
practices.safety: Structure for a habit you can safely change on your own, and nothing more — not treatment, and not a plan for physical dependence. If going without brings on shakes, sweating, nausea or bad anxiety, see a doctor before you change anything.

practices.title: Log the urge, not the verdict
practices.summary: Each evening, one line per urge — what happened, where you were, what you did — written before any judgement about it.
practices.why: Self-monitoring is one of the better-supported single ingredients in behaviour change. When researchers broke interventions into component techniques and asked which tracked with results, self-monitoring paired with a stated goal came out near the top across eating, activity and drinking. Two honest limits: it is almost never tested on its own, and people under-record, most reliably on the occasions they least want to write down — so a log is a floor, not a measurement. It earns its place because it is the fastest way to find that the real trigger is six o’clock and an empty house rather than stress, which is what nearly everyone assumes.
practices.safety: The log is data, never a scorecard, and IntentNorth does not charge for it. If what it shows you is daily use, amounts creeping upward, or that you cannot go a day without, that is a doctor’s conversation rather than a tracking problem.

practices.title: Monthly cue audit
practices.summary: Once a month, walk the rooms where it happens and change the place rather than the person — what is visible, what is within reach, what is in the house at all.
practices.why: Habits run on cues, and the most reliable way not to act on one is not to meet it. Field and laboratory work has moved how much people eat and drink by changing what is visible, how near it sits and what size it comes in, with nobody deciding to consume less. Removing a cue beats resisting it because resisting is expensive and unreliable: the people who score highest on self-control turn out mostly to be people who arrange their lives around fewer temptations, not people who win more fights with them. B rather than A because most trials are food and drink in controlled settings, effects are modest and short-run, and almost nobody has followed real households for a year.
practices.safety: Clearing the house is the right move for the phone, the biscuits, the app. It is not the move for alcohol if you drink every day: stopping abruptly after heavy daily drinking can be medically dangerous rather than merely unpleasant, and it needs a doctor’s supervision, not an empty cupboard.

practices.title: Ride the wave
practices.summary: When the urge lands, set five minutes: name it out loud, breathe slowly, and give your hands the replacement you chose in advance — no arguing with it.
practices.why: The idea is that an urge behaves like a wave: it rises, crests and falls whether or not you feed it, so the job is to stay with it rather than fight it. The pieces around it hold up reasonably — putting a feeling into words lowers its intensity, long exhales settle arousal, and having one rehearsed competing action beats having nothing to do with your hands. The direct evidence for urge surfing itself is thinner than the confidence with which it is taught: standalone studies are small, often single-session and mixed, and the good trials bundle it inside a whole programme. Treat the tidy “cravings last ten minutes” number as a clinical rule of thumb rather than a measured constant.
practices.safety: Riding out a craving is not the same as riding out withdrawal, and neither is a stand-in for professional help. Dependence on alcohol, drugs or gambling is a clinical matter: a doctor is the right first call, and free confidential helplines exist in most countries — a doctor or pharmacist can point you to the one where you live. IntentNorth’s urge support is free forever, and nothing here is ever locked.

practices.title: A lapse is one event
practices.summary: Within a day of a slip, ten written minutes: what the moment actually was, what you would change about the setup, and then the next ordinary day resumes — nothing restarts from zero.
practices.why: One slip rarely does the damage by itself. What predicts the collapse is the account given of it — that the run is dead, that this proves something permanent, so the rest of the night may as well go the same way. Rewriting it as a single event with a fixable cause keeps the next hour available. Graded C on purpose: the effect is well described and matches what people report, but the evidence is largely observational and retrospective, and no large trial has shown that changing the interpretation alone changes what happens next. Two things follow regardless: streak counters that reset to zero hand the story its ending, so IntentNorth does not keep one, and a lapse is information about the setup, which is the part you can change.
practices.safety: A written review is for an ordinary slip. If lapses are landing closer together or getting bigger, or one put you or somebody else in danger — driving, a hospital, money you could not afford to lose — that is past what a journal is for and belongs with a doctor or another professional. Free confidential helplines exist for drinking, drugs and gambling, and a doctor can point you to one.

practices.title: Days off, decided in advance
practices.summary: Every Monday, name which specific days this week are off — then take out what makes breaking them easy, and tell one person which days they are.
practices.why: Deciding in advance and then deliberately narrowing your own options later is a real mechanism with real trials behind it: randomised field experiments have shown people take up commitment contracts and change behaviour under them. Naming particular days rather than a weekly quantity does two useful things — it is checkable the next morning, and it ends the nightly negotiation about whether tonight counts. The evidence is thinner than the enthusiasm: uptake in those trials was low and gains faded once the contract ended. Be careful who you tell, too — there is experimental work suggesting that announcing a goal to people who approve can feel a little like having already achieved it, so tell one person who will ask you on Friday, not an audience.
practices.safety: Drink-free days are a structure for ordinary drinking. They are not a taper and not a medical plan. Daily drinking, symptoms on a day without one — shakes, sweating, nausea, a racing heart, bad anxiety — or an honest inability to stop once you have started, is a doctor’s job, and stopping abruptly after heavy daily use can be medically dangerous, seizures included. The same goes for gambling: it belongs with a professional, and free confidential helplines exist that cost nothing and ask for no name.

practices.title: One thing that still happens
practices.summary: Through a stretch where most of life has rearranged, keep exactly one small thing happening at the same time every day.
practices.why: When a lot changes at once, the case for holding one fixed point is that it costs almost nothing and gives an otherwise shapeless day an edge to start from. Be clear about how thin the support is: regular daily rhythms are associated with steadier mood in observational work, and rhythm stability is one ingredient inside therapy packages that work as packages, which tells you very little about the ingredient. Nobody has tested keeping one anchor against keeping none. This is experienced practice, and the reason to try it is that it asks so little.
practices.safety: Pick something small enough that a bad day cannot break it, and if this is the only thing that happens today, the day went fine. Structure for an ordinary hard stretch, not treatment and not a substitute for one. If weeks are passing and you cannot function, if hopelessness is not lifting, or if you are having thoughts of not wanting to be here, contact your doctor today.

practices.title: Make the plan smaller on purpose
practices.summary: Once a week during a hard stretch, cut the plan down to what you would still do on your worst day this week, and name the date you will look at it again.
practices.why: The best-replicated finding in this whole area is also the most reassuring one. When researchers follow large groups through bereavement, job loss, separation or disaster and look at individual trajectories rather than the average, much the largest group dips and then steadies without any intervention. Distress is ordinary and recovery is the norm. What that work does not support is a sequence: the familiar five-stages model has never held up when tested, and there is no evidence for a correct order, a correct length, or a point by which you should be somewhere else. So this does the one useful thing software can honestly do — it takes things off you, for a period you choose, and stops asking.
practices.safety: There is no schedule you are behind on and no right way to be doing this. Cutting the plan to almost nothing for a while is a reasonable answer, not a failure. This is scheduling structure and nothing else — not therapy, not counselling, and it does not assess how you are doing. If you cannot function after several weeks, if hopelessness or numbness is not shifting, or if you are having thoughts of not wanting to be here or of harming yourself, contact your doctor today; if it feels urgent, use your local emergency number or crisis line now.

practices.title: One small thing that matters
practices.summary: Plan one small act that matters to you the day before, and do it whether or not you feel like it when the time comes.
practices.why: Doing a small planned thing on a schedule rather than waiting to feel ready is the active ingredient in behavioural activation, which has strong randomised support. All of that support comes from the treatment of depression, which is not where this app stands, so we take only the non-clinical core and grade it for the use rather than for the trials. Motivation usually arrives after the action rather than before it, and in a stretch where nothing feels worth starting, ten planned minutes is a fairer test of that than an hour.
practices.safety: Small means small — a shower, a walk to the corner, one email. If planning it makes the day worse, drop it; a skipped day carries no meaning and nothing here is a measure of how you are coping. Not a stand-in for care: if you have been unable to function for weeks, or hopelessness is not lifting, that is a conversation with your doctor.

practices.title: One person, once a week
practices.summary: One contact a week with one person who already knows what is going on — a call, a walk, a sat-down coffee.
practices.why: Of everything measured in this literature, the strength of someone’s connections is the most consistent protective factor for how they come through a hard stretch, and it holds across large cohorts followed for years. Two honest caveats: almost all of it is observational, so support and doing well travel together without the arrow being settled; and the direction that replicates best is people needing others more than they expect while assuming, wrongly, that they would be a burden.
practices.safety: One person is the whole target, and sitting together saying nothing counts. Nobody has to talk it through, and there is no benefit to be had from being made to. If the honest answer is that there is no one, that is worth saying to your doctor, who can point you at bereavement or support services near you.

practices.title: Write from a value
practices.summary: Ten minutes writing about one value that genuinely matters to you and a specific time you acted on it — best used the evening before something hard.
practices.why: This is the most tested writing exercise in the area. Across a long run of randomised experiments, people who spent a few minutes writing about a value they hold went into a stressful or ego-threatening situation less defensive, with smaller stress responses and a readier ear for unwelcome information. It is B rather than A because the effect is context-dependent — timing matters, the writing has to be about the value rather than a list of them, and several widely repeated long-run results came out smaller in larger replications. Which value it is appears to matter far less than the fact that it is honestly yours.
practices.safety: IntentNorth has no view on where your values come from or what they should be — the exercise works on whatever you already hold, and the app never supplies the list. It is also not a way to write around a real problem. If the honest answer on the page is that nothing much matters any more, or that has been true for weeks, that belongs with a doctor or a therapist rather than a journal.

practices.title: What am I actually for
practices.summary: Once a quarter, forty-five minutes on three written questions: what you want to be true in five years, who your ordinary week actually serves, and the one thing you would change first.
practices.why: Large prospective studies following tens of thousands of adults find that people who report a strong sense of purpose die later and have fewer heart events than people who do not, and the association survives the obvious adjustments. It is a real finding and still only an association: healthier, better-connected, less depressed people find purpose easier to report, and — the part usually left out — nobody has shown that manufacturing a sense of purpose on demand changes any of those outcomes. Strong cohorts, untested practice. What a quarterly review can honestly offer is narrower: noticing early that your weeks have drifted away from what you say you care about.
practices.safety: A review, never a verdict — plenty of good lives do not resolve into a single sentence, and being unable to name a purpose is not a diagnosis of anything. Do not read the mortality research as a warning aimed at you: it describes groups, not your next decade. If the sitting leaves you with weeks of flatness or hopelessness, that is a doctor or therapist conversation now rather than a question to leave for the next quarter.

practices.title: One deliberate contribution
practices.summary: Once a month, one concrete act for someone outside your own household — money given on purpose to a named cause or person, or a few hours of real help arranged in advance.
practices.why: The controlled part is spending: hand people a small amount of money, randomly assign some to spend it on someone else, and the ones who did report better mood by the end of the day. That has repeated in several countries, in rich and poor settings and with young children, which is unusual for a wellbeing finding — though effects are modest and some later replications came out smaller. The volunteering half is weaker and worth saying plainly: volunteers report better health and mood, but almost all of that is observational and volunteers are healthier and better connected to begin with. What the experiments suggest is that vagueness kills it — a specific recipient beats an anonymous transfer.
practices.safety: Give from what you can spare. If a regular gift would put your own bills or repayments under strain, size it with a licensed financial adviser before you commit, and never as a way to feel better about money that is already tight. Hours given to people who are unwell, elderly or under eighteen should go through an organisation that does proper checks and training.

practices.title: Best possible self
practices.summary: Roughly fortnightly, fifteen minutes writing in detail about a year from now in which things have gone about as well as they realistically could — then one concrete step you would take this month.
practices.why: Small randomised experiments have compared this with neutral writing and found short-term lifts in mood and optimism, fairly consistently across a few labs. The caveats are the usual ones: small samples, brief follow-ups, self-reported outcomes and very little evidence that anything holds beyond a few weeks. It is included because it does something the rest of this group does not — makes a wanted future specific enough to act on. The step at the end is not decoration: separate work on imagined futures suggests that dwelling on a pleasant fantasy without confronting what stands in the way can quietly drain the effort to pursue it.
practices.safety: Realistically as well as it could go, not a fantasy — the exercise loses its point when the page describes a life that was never available. If imagining a good year mostly produces a list of what you have already lost, or leaves you reliably worse than you started, stop and take that to a doctor or therapist rather than writing through it.

practices.title: The thank-you letter
practices.summary: Once a month, a letter to one person about something specific they actually did for you — and, where you can face it, read it to them.
practices.why: The much-quoted result is a randomised trial in which writing and then delivering a letter of thanks produced the largest short-term happiness bump of the exercises tested — and in the same paper it had faded within a few months, against a control doing very little. Later meta-analyses of gratitude exercises land on small effects, mostly self-reported. What has held up more robustly is a smaller, stranger finding: senders consistently underestimate how much a message like this lands, and overestimate how awkward it will be, which is exactly the miscalculation that stops people sending them.
practices.safety: Written and not sent still counts — delivery is the stronger version, not an obligation, and nobody is owed a letter. If the person who comes to mind is someone who hurt you, this exercise is not the place to work that out; a therapist is.

practices.title: An if-then plan for the window that goes wrong
practices.summary: Ten Sunday minutes writing one line for the window food goes sideways — “if it’s 9pm and I’m on the sofa, then I make tea”.
practices.why: Naming the situation, the time and the first physical move is among the best-replicated findings in behaviour-change research. Pooled across roughly two dozen eating trials the technique shifts behaviour meaningfully — and it is notably stronger for adding something than for subtracting something. So the line has to end in a move you make, not a thing you resist: “then I make tea”, never “then I don’t snack”.
practices.safety: A plan for one window, not a verdict on the evening. If eating in that window feels genuinely out of control, a GP or a dietitian will do more than any if-then line.

practices.title: Plate up in the kitchen
practices.summary: Serve onto plates in the kitchen and leave the pans there; anything from a packet goes into a bowl first.
practices.why: What is put in front of you is what gets eaten. A Cochrane review of 61 randomised comparisons in about 6,700 people found people reliably eat more when handed a larger portion or package, and the effect did not vary much by sex, body size or hunger. Serving at the hob and decanting from the packet make the first helping the default; a second helping is still there, it just costs a decision. Note what this is not: the separate claim that smaller plates make you eat less is much weaker, and a pre-registered trial found nothing.
practices.safety: This is about where the serving dish sits, not about eating less than you need. Training hard, pregnant, unwell, or losing weight you did not mean to lose — then the bigger first plate is the right one.

practices.title: Change what is in reach
practices.summary: Once a week, move whatever you graze on out of eye-line, and put cut fruit at the front of the fridge instead.
practices.why: Distance is friction, and friction is most of the decision. A Cochrane review found food placed further away was eaten less — a moderate pooled effect across twelve studies — but graded its own evidence low certainty, because it rests on short laboratory sittings with small samples. Hence C, not B. The swap matters as much as the removal: the if-then literature is clearly better at getting a food in than at keeping a food out, and a visible fruit bowl is the “in” half. What we deliberately do not lean on is the claim that you can read someone’s weight off their kitchen counter — that traces to a retracted body of work.
practices.safety: Rearranging a kitchen is a small thing and should stay one. If what may or may not be in the house starts to feel like a rule you are not allowed to break, if it makes eating with other people hard, or if food is already something you fight with, stop this protocol and speak to a GP, a registered dietitian or an eating-disorder service. A food environment held rigidly can become part of the problem rather than a way out of it.

practices.title: Eat away from the screen
practices.summary: Food gets eaten sitting down, away from the TV and the phone — the evening snack in front of a box set included.
practices.why: The honest version is narrower than the popular one. Two independent meta-analyses, of 23 and 50 experiments, agree that distraction barely moves how much you eat during the meal itself — the pooled effect is small and not clearly different from zero. What it does move is the NEXT eating occasion, modestly but consistently, and television is the distraction that shows it most clearly. The likely mechanism is memory: a meal you never attended to is a meal your appetite does not fully count a few hours later.
practices.safety: Attention, not restriction. This is about noticing the food, and it is not a reason to skip a meal or eat less than you need.

practices.title: The kitchen shutdown
practices.summary: A short closing routine each evening — wash up, wipe down, light off — so the kitchen has visibly finished for the day.
practices.why: Sister to “Kitchen closes”, which sets the TIME; this sets the CUE. Evening eating is usually triggered rather than hungry, and a meta-analysis covering some 3,300 people found food cue reactivity and craving track how much people go on to eat — track, not proven to cause. Taking the cue away is long-standing practice inside multi-component behavioural programmes, but it has almost never been tested on its own, which is exactly what a D means here.
practices.safety: A closed kitchen is a signal, not a lock. If you are genuinely hungry after it, eat. A rule that overrides hunger has stopped being a habit, and that is worth raising with a GP or a registered dietitian.

practices.title: The cycle and symptom log
practices.summary: A short daily line: where you are in your cycle if you track it, plus energy, sleep, soreness and any symptoms as they actually were.
practices.why: Cycle-related symptoms are common, vary enormously between people, and almost none of your own pattern is visible from memory — asked a month later, people reconstruct rather than recall, which is why menstrual-symptom research collects daily diaries instead of questionnaires. A dated log turns that into something you can read: which days reliably cost you, whether something is drifting across months, what to take to a doctor. What no study shows is that logging by itself makes anyone train better or feel better — the log is raw material for your own decisions.
practices.safety: A private record, never a forecast and never an assessment: IntentNorth cannot tell you what a pattern means, cannot predict a cycle, and has nothing to say about contraception, conception or any medication — those belong with a doctor. Periods that are very heavy or very painful, bleeding that has newly changed, or symptoms that flatten you every month are a doctor’s question rather than something to log around.

practices.title: Train to symptoms, not to a phase template
practices.summary: Before each session, read your own log and set today’s effort from how you actually feel — not from which week of the cycle it is.
practices.why: This is where the popular version and the evidence part company. Systematic reviews pooling the cycle-phase performance studies find group-level effects on strength and endurance too small and too inconsistent to plan around, and rate most of the underlying work low quality. A template that says lift heavy this week and back off next week is applying an average that may not describe you at all. What is not in doubt is that some people get symptoms that genuinely change what a session should be that day, and that those patterns are individual — an argument for your own record, not for a calendar rule. Regular exercise also has modest randomised support for easing period pain, so the honest move on a bad day is usually a smaller session rather than none.
practices.safety: Information, not a limitation and not an excuse — most sessions on most days are ordinary sessions, and this protocol has no opinion about what you are capable of. Adjusting effort is different from training through something wrong: pain that stops you, bleeding that soaks through hourly, or any symptom that is new or worsening is a doctor’s question rather than a programming one.

practices.title: Load through the transition
practices.summary: Two properly heavy resistance sessions a week through the years around menopause — compound lifts, progressed on purpose, plus impact work if it suits you.
practices.why: Bone and muscle both come under pressure in the years either side of the last period, and the usual instinct is to train more gently — which is the wrong direction. Supervised trials of progressive high-load resistance and impact training in postmenopausal women improved bone density at the hip and spine along with strength and everyday function, where light and moderate programmes largely did not. Two limits stated honestly: those trials measured density and strength, not broken bones; and they were supervised, with technique coached before the weight went up. What survives both caveats is the direction of travel — the case for loading gets stronger through this period, not weaker.
practices.safety: Progressive means across months, technique before weight, and coaching is worth more here than almost anywhere else. Known osteoporosis or low bone density, a previous fragility fracture, or back, hip or joint trouble changes what loading is appropriate — that is a doctor or physiotherapist call before you start. IntentNorth says nothing at all about hormone therapy, medication or supplements. Broken sleep through this period is common and real: the wind-down, anchored wake time and twenty-minute-rule protocols are the behavioural tools for it, and months of bad nights belong with a doctor.

practices.title: Pelvic floor practice
practices.summary: A daily set of pelvic floor contractions — a few short hard squeezes and a few long holds, done properly rather than done often.
practices.why: One of the strongest behavioural findings in this library, and one of the least likely to appear in a general fitness app. Pooled randomised trials find women doing pelvic floor muscle training are far more likely to report leaking gone or improved than women given no such training, with the clearest effect in stress incontinence — it is the first-line recommendation in clinical guidelines internationally, ahead of anything surgical. The caveat is about delivery rather than the finding: those trials taught the contraction in person and checked that people had found it, and a substantial share of women practising unsupervised are doing something else entirely. An app can hold the habit and the cadence. It cannot see whether you are contracting the right muscles, which is the part that makes the evidence apply to you.
practices.safety: Learn the contraction from a pelvic health physiotherapist first — that is what makes the evidence transfer, and it is the necessary step if leaking, heaviness, pain, or anything that changed after a birth is part of the picture. Those things are assessed by a clinician; IntentNorth assesses nothing. Stop if the practice itself hurts. After a birth, begin what your midwife or doctor clears at your postnatal check and follow their timing over ours.

practices.title: Keep moving — on your clinician’s terms
practices.summary: Ask your midwife, obstetrician or doctor what activity suits your pregnancy or your recovery, then hold the smallest version of it — usually a daily walk you can talk through.
practices.why: Guidelines across several countries converge: in an uncomplicated pregnancy, regular moderate activity is beneficial rather than risky, and the pooled trials behind them point to lower odds of gestational diabetes and of excessive weight gain, with no signal of harm. That is a statement about populations. Whether it describes you depends on things only your maternity team knows, and the guidelines are built around individual clearance for exactly that reason. So we ship the two parts we can honestly hold: the prompt to have the conversation, and a habit small enough to survive a trimester or a newborn. What IntentNorth will never do is write you a programme.
practices.safety: Your midwife, obstetrician or doctor decides what is safe for your pregnancy and for your recovery afterwards. IntentNorth does not know your history and cannot know it, and this protocol has no view on intensity, load, position, or how far along you are — their instructions replace anything here, including this note. Stop and contact your maternity team for bleeding, fluid leaking, regular painful contractions, chest pain, calf pain or swelling, dizziness or headache. After a birth, nothing restarts before your postnatal check clears it.

practices.title: The same bedtime, the same order
practices.summary: Run the same short sequence at the same time every night — bath or wash, pyjamas, story, lights out.
practices.why: Randomised trials of consistent bedtime routines in young children report faster sleep onset, fewer night wakings and calmer evenings within a couple of weeks. What seems to carry the effect is the sameness — same steps, same order, same clock — rather than which steps you pick.
practices.safety: Educational structure, never medical advice. Hold it warmly: a sequence enforced against a frightened or distressed child has stopped being a routine, and an off night is an off night, not a verdict on you. If sleep is a lasting worry — loud snoring or pauses in breathing, tiredness that never lifts, or a child repeatedly terrified at night — that belongs with your GP or health visitor rather than with a better schedule.

practices.title: Ten minutes they lead
practices.summary: Ten minutes of play the child controls completely, where you describe what they are doing instead of directing, questioning or correcting.
practices.why: Child-directed play is the first skill taught in the parenting programmes with the strongest trial record, and dropping instructions and questions for a few minutes is the part parents find hardest. It is almost always tested inside a full programme rather than alone, so the component has thinner support than the programme does. Where the weekly one-to-one is about finding the time, this is about what you do with the minutes.
practices.safety: Ordinary play, not therapy, and not a way of managing behaviour in the moment. Follow rather than steer, and stop when they are finished — play a child has to complete has lost the point of itself. If something about your child’s behaviour or development worries you over time, a GP or health visitor can point you to a properly delivered programme; ten minutes at home is no substitute for one.

practices.title: Say exactly what they did
practices.summary: For the first ten minutes you are back together, name the specific thing the child did rather than saying “well done”.
practices.why: Describing the behaviour you want more of gives the child information that a generic “good boy” does not, and it is a component of every well-trialled parenting programme. Head-to-head comparisons of specific against generic praise are small and short. Note that the popular claim about praising effort rather than ability has had a mixed replication record, so take the specific version as a sane default, not a technique with a big effect behind it.
practices.safety: Warmth, not a reward economy. The line is approval that has to be earned: praise handed out to steer a child, or pointedly withheld while you are annoyed, does something different from praise given because you noticed. Some children dislike being singled out in front of others — quiet and specific works just as well.

practices.title: You go first
practices.summary: Five minutes before the hardest hour of the day, rehearse the pause: one long breath out, then the sentence you actually want to reach for.
practices.why: Every trialled parenting programme assumes the adult settles first, and slowing the out-breath measurably takes the edge off arousal in adult studies. Whether rehearsing it beforehand changes how the evening goes has not been tested directly in parents, so this is a mechanism borrowed and applied rather than a trial result — plausible, and honestly thin.
practices.safety: A pause means a breath before you speak. It is not silence aimed at a child, not walking out on one who needs you, and not affection switched off until they behave — when a young child is distressed, staying with them comes first. Every parent loses their temper sometimes and it does not undo a relationship. If your own anger frightens you, or you dread being alone with your child, that is worth raising with your GP, and support lines exist for exactly this.

practices.title: Settle the screen rules once
practices.summary: Roughly monthly, twenty-five minutes writing down where, when and how screens happen — then stop renegotiating it daily.
practices.why: Households with settled media rules report less use and slightly better child sleep, though that is observational. Be careful here: the harm evidence is far weaker and more contested than the public conversation suggests, and the largest re-analyses put the association between screen time and adolescent wellbeing at close to nothing. The defensible reason for a rule is displacement — screens eat sleep, meals and going outside — so write it to protect those, and worry less about the total hours.
practices.safety: An agreement written with the children old enough to be part of it, not a sanction handed down. Confiscation used as a punishment tends to make the device the most valuable thing in the house. What a child sees and who they talk to online matters more than minutes on a clock: if you are worried about either, that is a safeguarding conversation with your school, GP or a children’s charity, not a scheduling problem.

practices.title: Rehearse out loud, across days
practices.summary: With a talk coming, run it aloud from memory for twenty minutes on three separate days rather than once the night before.
practices.why: Two things underneath this are as well tested as anything in the library: pulling material out of your head beats reading it again, and the same minutes spread across days beat the same minutes in one sitting. Saying it aloud adds a smaller, well-replicated effect of its own. What nobody has tested is the package — no trial shows that three spaced out-loud run-throughs produce a better-rated talk than one long night before it. Strong mechanisms, untested application, so the claim stays narrow: you will need the notes less, which is most of what makes a talk sound like a person talking.
practices.safety: Preparation for ordinary nerves. If the fear of speaking is shaping what you take on — work turned down, rooms avoided, weeks lost to dread — that is worth taking to a doctor or a therapist rather than rehearsing through, and it is a common thing they help people with.

practices.title: One small speaking rep a week
practices.summary: Every week, one voluntary speaking turn small enough to be survivable: a question asked aloud, a two-minute update, the first comment in the room.
practices.why: Every intervention that reliably reduces speaking fear has the same thing inside it — doing the feared thing repeatedly, in sizes you can stay in, without leaving early. Controlled trials find graded repeated practice reduces speaking fear, and it beats the reassurance-and-tips format most workplace training is built from. Two honest limits: that work is mostly guided by a therapist, in people whose fear was strong enough to enrol them in a trial, and a rep you spend hiding at the back is avoidance in the practice’s clothing. Frequency does the work — a small rep every week beats a big one every quarter.
practices.safety: Ordinary nerves fade as the reps stack up. Fear that is limiting your life rather than just spoiling your morning — turning down work, avoiding people, weeks of dread before a routine meeting — is not a volume problem, and a doctor or therapist is the right next step rather than a harder rep. Pushing through panic is not the practice.

practices.title: One filmed run-through, one cue
practices.summary: Film two minutes of the talk on your phone, write down beforehand what you expect to see, then watch it once against a single cue.
practices.why: What a talk feels like and what it looks like drift apart quickly, and video is the cheapest way to close that gap. On its own it mostly hands a nervous speaker more material for the case they were already making against themselves. The narrower finding is the useful one: with anxious speakers, watching yourself back helped when it followed forming a concrete picture of what you expected to see, and did much less without that step. Past that it is rumination with a play button.
practices.safety: Watch it once, against the one cue you wrote, then stop — repeat viewings reliably make people feel worse without making the talk better. If you cannot watch it without spiralling, that is worth saying to a professional rather than solving with more footage.

practices.title: Write the opening line
practices.summary: Before a conversation you are dreading, write the first two sentences you will actually say, word for word, and the outcome you want from it.
practices.why: Deciding in advance exactly what you will do and when is among the better-supported behaviour findings there is, and it is already in this library as if-then planning. Writing the first two sentences applies that mechanism where these conversations usually go wrong: an unplanned opening either softens into nothing or arrives as an accusation, and everything after it is spent recovering. Nothing tests this specific practice, so the grade is for a strong mechanism carried somewhere it has not been measured. The rest is craft — name the thing, say plainly why it matters to you, ask how they see it, then stop talking.
practices.safety: Preparation changes how you open, never how it lands. Anything involving conduct, safety, pay or someone’s job belongs in your employer’s formal process, and a rehearsed sentence is not the place to raise it first. If you are dreading it because the other person has been threatening or abusive, that is a conversation to have with support, not alone.

practices.title: Say it back before you answer
practices.summary: Once a week, in one real conversation, say the other person’s point back in your own words until they agree you have it — then reply.
practices.why: This is the most widely taught communication behaviour there is and one of the most thinly evidenced outside the clinic. What holds up: across many trials of counselling for behaviour change, reflective and empathic responding by the practitioner tracks with better outcomes. What does not: the same technique packaged as a couples drill fared badly when couples were followed for years. In workplaces the studies are small, single-conversation and self-rated, mostly showing people feel more understood. A real mechanism — you cannot answer an argument you have not understood — and no strong outcome evidence at work.
practices.safety: Said back as a technique it reads as one, and people notice. Use it to check you have understood, not to win — and if the other person asks you to stop narrating them, stop.

practices.title: If-then the three that always slip
practices.summary: Ten Sunday minutes turning the three admin jobs that keep sliding into “when I am at X doing Y, I will do Z”.
practices.why: A to-do list records what you intend; an if-then plan records where and when the doing starts. Specifying the exact opportunity — the cue, the place, the first physical move — is among the best-replicated findings in behaviour-change research, and largest for precisely the intentions that keep failing. Two honest limits: it does little for a task you do not genuinely mean to do, and it fades when the goal was someone else’s. Name the opportunity, not the hour: “when the kettle goes on Tuesday” beats “Tuesday morning”, because a kettle happens and a morning is negotiable.

practices.title: Every renewal date, out of your head
practices.summary: Once a quarter, forty minutes putting every renewal, expiry and deadline you own into one dated store, each with a reminder set weeks before it bites.
practices.why: Remembering to do something months from now is what human memory is worst at, and the fix is not effort — it is writing it somewhere you will be told. Experiments on cognitive offloading are unusually clean: people who hand a to-be-remembered item to an external store perform better on whatever they do next, and the freed attention is measurable rather than merely reported. One result matters most for how you build this — the benefit collapses when the store turns out to be unreliable, because a system you do not trust gets silently duplicated in your head. Hence one place, not five. Nobody has trialled a quarterly sweep, so read that part as reasonable rather than shown.
practices.safety: One store, and keep the sensitive documents themselves out of it — a list of dates does not need passport numbers or account details sitting beside it. Anything with legal or immigration consequences deserves a real reminder and a professional, not a calendar entry alone.

practices.title: The visible household list
practices.summary: One list everyone in the house can see of the recurring jobs, a single name beside each, reviewed together for five minutes at the start of the week.
practices.why: Decades of time-use research describe the same asymmetry: the visible half of running a household gets shared far more evenly than the invisible half, which is noticing that a thing is due, deciding what to do about it, and carrying it until it is done. That half leaves no trace, so it is hard to see and easy to under-count in whoever is not doing it. The evidence is consistent and entirely observational, and no study has shown that writing a list changes how the work lands. What is sound is the reasoning: labour nobody can see cannot be negotiated. Put the noticing in the name, not just the doing.
practices.safety: A list of who owns what, never a scoreboard of who does more — the second version reliably starts the argument the first one was meant to prevent. If the same imbalance keeps coming back however it is written down, that is a conversation about the arrangement, and sometimes one for a couples therapist, rather than a better board.

practices.title: The weekly admin block
practices.summary: Forty-five minutes at the same hour every week for the paperwork — one list, worst first, and you stop when the timer stops.
practices.why: Batching similar jobs into one sitting is sensible-sounding and thinly tested. The switching-cost literature it leans on is real but modest and mostly small laboratory studies, and nobody has run the obvious comparison. So the claim is deliberately small. What the block reliably buys is a place to put things down, and one decision made once instead of forty times a week. Two design notes from practice rather than data: worst first, because the dreaded item would otherwise consume the whole hour in advance, and a hard stop, because an admin block with no end quietly becomes the evening.
practices.safety: Anything needing an office to be open cannot live in an evening block — give those their own daytime line instead of watching them roll over for a month. And forty-five minutes is forty-five minutes: a backlog built of debt letters, benefits, immigration or probate paperwork is structural, and free advice services and licensed professionals exist for exactly that.

practices.title: Set the launch pad
practices.summary: Ten minutes before bed setting up tomorrow’s first hour: what you leave with by the door, one surface cleared to start on.
practices.why: The dependable half of a calm house is not resolve, it is what is visible, reachable and already arranged. Field experiments on defaults and placement shift behaviour more reliably than reminders or willpower do, and that is the same lever behind parking the phone in another room. Setting the first hour of tomorrow tonight points it at your own morning. The support is for the mechanism, not for this particular ritual: nobody has trialled a launch pad.

practices.title: Fifteen minutes, one surface
practices.summary: A timer set for fifteen minutes on one named surface — the kitchen table, the desk, the chair by the door — and you stop when it goes.
practices.why: What holds up here is general rather than domestic: a specific bounded target, and watching progress accumulate, make people more likely to finish a large job than an open-ended intention to sort it all out eventually. That comes from meta-analytic work on goal setting and progress monitoring, none of it run on garages, so we are borrowing it on purpose. Naming one surface is what stops the session quietly becoming the whole house and therefore never happening. We are not telling you a tidy home makes a tidy mind — that claim is folklore with unusually good marketing.
practices.safety: For some people, parting with things is genuinely distressing rather than merely tedious — enough that rooms stop being usable. Difficulty discarding possessions is a recognised clinical condition with real help available, and it belongs with your doctor rather than with a tidying schedule. IntentNorth cannot tell which situation you are in and this is not an assessment. Never run a pass on someone else’s belongings without their agreement.

practices.title: One month banked before anything else
practices.summary: Until one month of expenses is sitting somewhere you can reach, the automatic transfer goes there and nowhere else.
practices.why: Households with even a small cash buffer report less financial stress and are far less likely to sell investments or borrow at high rates when a car or a tooth breaks; that comes from large surveys in several countries, consistent but observational. Australian government guidance suggests three months as the target. The first month does most of the work: it turns an emergency back into an inconvenience.
practices.safety: Where the buffer sits, a savings account, an offset account against a home loan, or somewhere else, depends on your loan, your tax and how quickly you may need it, and that is a licensed adviser or accountant question. Education, never financial advice.

practices.title: A target with an amount and a date
practices.summary: Write the amount, the date and what is there now, and let the coach turn it into a monthly figure and dated steps.
practices.why: A large study of savers on a banking app found that people who set a specific saving goal put away more than matched users who did not, and the effect held up when the same people were compared before and after setting one. That sits on decades of goal-setting research: a specific, dated target with feedback beats a vague intention. Sub-goals help most early, when the first small step is close, so the steps start at the first thousand rather than at a quarter of the way.
practices.safety: The monthly figure is arithmetic on the numbers you give, not a forecast of returns, and it assumes no interest unless you enter a rate. Whether the target itself is the right use of the money is a licensed adviser conversation. Education, never financial advice.

practices.title: Know the student loan date before paying extra
practices.summary: Once a year, before June, look at your student loan (HELP) balance, the indexation rate and whether a voluntary payment is worth it that year at all.
practices.why: An Australian student loan carries no interest but is indexed once a year on 1 June, and compulsory repayments come out of pay above a threshold. That shape is why the usual order puts it after a cash buffer and after any expensive debt: a voluntary payment only changes anything if it lands before indexation, and a buffer or a card balance usually matters more. This is arithmetic from the published rules rather than a trial of anything.
practices.safety: Whether a voluntary payment beats keeping the money elsewhere depends on your income, your other debts and the year’s indexation, and an accountant or licensed adviser can run your numbers. The thresholds and rates change each year; check the government site rather than a memory of them. Education, never financial advice.

practices.title: Creatine, the plain kind
practices.summary: If you lift, a small daily amount of plain creatine monohydrate — the same every day, training day or not.
practices.why: The most-tested sports supplement there is. Hundreds of trials and a position stand from the International Society of Sports Nutrition find a little more strength and lean mass from resistance training once muscle creatine stores are full, and no harm to kidney function in healthy adults across years of use. The stand describes three to five grams a day filling the stores over three to four weeks; a bigger loading week is faster, not better. Without training there is little to show for it, and plain monohydrate is the form the evidence used — the expensive variants have not beaten it.
practices.safety: An existing kidney condition changes the picture entirely — that is a doctor’s call, not this card’s. A kilo or so of water in the first weeks is normal and is not fat. Education, never advice: nothing here tells you to take anything, and no amount on this card outranks a label or a professional. Talk to a doctor or pharmacist before starting anything — especially if you take any medication, because interactions are real; if you are pregnant or breastfeeding; if you have a kidney or liver condition; or if you have any history of disordered eating.
attribution: International Society of Sports Nutrition (Kreider et al., 2017)

practices.title: Protein powder is food, not a supplement
practices.summary: Use a scoop of protein powder as a convenient part of a meal when whole food is short — never as the plan.
practices.why: A tub of whey or pea protein is a food with the water taken out. The evidence behind it is the protein target itself: the position stand puts exercising adults at roughly 1.4 to 2 grams per kilogram a day and finds no advantage for powder over meat, eggs, dairy or beans once the total is met. What a scoop buys is convenience — a fourth feed on a training day, a breakfast that would otherwise be toast. The stand prefers whole foods wherever they are available, and so does this plan.
practices.safety: Whey is milk, and many pea and soy powders carry allergen warnings — read the label if you have an allergy, because the dish model here excludes nothing on your behalf. Kidney disease, or a doctor’s existing advice about protein, outranks any target. Education, never advice: nothing here tells you to take anything, and no amount on this card outranks a label or a professional.
