The best review of dry-sauna trials says plainly that the evidence cannot yet tell the two apart, which means nothing shows infrared is worse and nothing yet shows it earns the Finnish numbers. So take the part that is real — the ritual, the warmth, the sleep-friendly wind-down when it ends early enough — and let the research catch up.
practices.safety: Same care as any heat: water before and after, alcohol nowhere near it, out at the first dizziness, and a doctor first if you are pregnant, have a heart condition, or take medication that affects blood pressure, sweating or body temperature. Educational structure, not medical advice.

practices.title: Find your own number
practices.summary: On any morning you wake without an alarm, jot down how long you slept. After a few weeks of those mornings, the middle of the pile is your number — and it is probably not eight.
practices.why: The consensus bodies say seven to nine hours for adults; "eight" was never their figure. Need really does vary: in a laboratory study that gave fifteen young men nights of unlimited sleep, their settled requirement ran from about seven and a quarter hours to nine and a quarter. Alarm-free mornings are the free version of that experiment, and a Sunday is when most people get one. Knowing your number turns every other sleep decision — bedtime, the caffeine cutoff, whether a short night matters — from a guess into arithmetic.
practices.safety: An estimate from a small study, not a measurement, and a holiday week gives a cleaner read than scattered weekends. Regularly sleeping ten hours and still feeling flattened, or nodding off without meaning to, is worth raising with a doctor.

practices.title: The Sunday sleep ledger
practices.summary: Once a week, five minutes: add up the hours you actually had available for sleep over the last seven nights, count the broken ones, and decide the week from the total rather than from how you feel.
practices.why: The useful surprise from the sleep-restriction trials is that how sleepy you feel stops tracking how impaired you are: across two weeks on six hours a night, reaction times kept getting worse while people’s own rating of their sleepiness levelled off after a few days. So the tally is the instrument. What it tells you is simple. A short week is repaid over several earlier nights with the wake time held — one long lie-in does not settle it, and a weekend recovered about an hour in the one trial that measured it. A run of broken nights that has lasted most of three months is the signal to book a GP and ask about cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia, the best-evidenced thing in this whole pillar and one an app cannot deliver. Everything else is a good week, and you get to see that too.
practices.safety: A weekly total under your number for more than a few weeks is a reason to change the week, not to try harder. If the hours are there and the sleep is not, or you snore loudly, gasp in the night, or fall asleep in the day, see a doctor or sleep clinician — the insomnia programme they can refer you to works, and this ledger is only the thing that tells you it is time.

practices.title: The anchor: four hours at the same clock time
practices.summary: Through a run of nights and the days off around it, protect one four-hour block of sleep at the same clock time every day, in a blacked-out, cool, quiet room, and let the rest of your sleep land wherever it fits.
practices.why: The body clock does not need all your sleep at the same time; it needs some of it to be. In isolation-unit experiments, people whose sleep was scattered drifted off a 24-hour day, and holding just one four-hour block at a fixed time pulled them back within days regardless of what they did with the other half. Laboratory studies since then find split sleep costs nothing against one long block when the total matches. The research is old and small and the practice is what makes a rotating week hold together: one thing that never moves, and everything else is allowed to.
practices.safety: A roster that leaves no four-hour block at a stable time is a workplace problem, not a personal failing, and worth raising as one. Falling asleep at the wheel or on the job is a same-week conversation with your employer and your doctor.

practices.title: Bright light through the first half of the night
practices.summary: On nights, give yourself bright light — a light box, or the brightest room in the building — for fifteen to twenty minutes every hour or so through the first half to two-thirds of the shift, then let it fade for the last hours.
practices.why: Light is what moves the clock, and on a night shift the clock is pointing the wrong way. In a controlled study of sixty-seven people on simulated nights, bright light through the shift plus dark glasses for the trip home and a fixed dark day sleep re-set the clock almost completely within five shifts; in nineteen real nurses the same package moved their rhythms nine to eleven hours against four or five for the control group. The light is the part you can do at work, and it is the part that makes the day sleep come easily instead of being fought for. Stopping it before the shift ends is on purpose: the aim is a clock that is sleepy by mid-morning and still workable on days off.
practices.safety: Bright light and some conditions or medications do not mix — retinal disease, bipolar disorder and photosensitising drugs are a doctor’s call before you start. The light box tells your clock what time you would like it to be; it is not a treatment for anything.

practices.title: Dark glasses from the door to the bed
practices.summary: After a night shift, very dark or orange-tinted glasses go on before you step outside and stay on until the bedroom door — even under cloud.
practices.why: Morning light after a night shift is the loudest possible instruction to the body clock to stay on day time, which is exactly what the coming day sleep does not need. The glasses are one third of the package that re-set the clock in the laboratory and in nurses and police officers, and in the lab the darkest lenses did most of the work when no light box was used. Cheap, silly-looking and effective: most people who try it once notice the day sleep arrives faster.
practices.safety: Glasses dark enough to work are too dark to drive in. Wear them as a passenger, on the train, or on foot.

practices.title: Not driving home
practices.summary: After a night shift, get home some other way if there is any other way; if there is none, a short nap before you leave and the shortest route there is.
practices.why: This is the one shift-work finding that should change a decision on its own, and it is a kindness to yourself rather than a rule. Sixteen shift workers drove a real car on a closed track for two hours after a night shift and again after a night’s sleep: after the shift, six had near-crashes and seven had to be stopped by the safety observer; after sleep, none of either. Lane drift doubled and eyes stayed closed measurably longer per blink. One study, one track, and consistent with every drowsy-driving record ever kept. A lift, a train, a taxi or twenty minutes asleep in the car park are all cheaper than the alternative.
practices.safety: A nap before driving lowers the risk without removing it. Falling asleep at the wheel is a workplace safety matter as well as a personal one, and it is fair to raise it that way.

practices.title: The evening nap before the first night
practices.summary: Before the first night or two of a run, a sixty-to-ninety-minute nap in the early evening, two or three hours before you leave. Even forty minutes helps.
practices.why: In a laboratory trial of sixty-eight people and a field study of fifty-three real night workers, an evening nap before the first nights of a run — with or without coffee early in the shift — measurably improved alertness and reaction time through the night, and the two together worked best. It is the best-supported shift-work countermeasure the Cochrane reviewers could find. The front of the run is where the clock is furthest from where the shift needs it, and this is the cheapest thing that helps there.
practices.safety: Give yourself an hour between waking and needing to be sharp: a nap this long ends in deep sleep and the grogginess after it is real. Skip it while you are working through insomnia with a clinician.

practices.title: One short nap at the low point
practices.summary: One nap on the night shift, around three or four in the morning: ten to twenty minutes if you need to be sharp the moment you wake, thirty if you have a clear half hour afterwards.
practices.why: A pooled analysis of thirteen studies found naps on nights reliably cut end-of-shift sleepiness, and the biggest workplace study, in 109 nurses, found a thirty-minute nap at four a.m. improved both how they felt and how they performed through to seven. The one thing to plan is the waking: in the laboratory a thirty-minute night nap left people foggy for about forty-five minutes, and a ten-minute nap did not, because the short one ends before deep sleep begins. One nap, not two — two showed no extra benefit. Ten minutes with your eyes closed in the break room is a real intervention, and it feels like one.
practices.safety: The half hour after a longer nap is the fuzzy window: no driving, no machinery, no big decisions until it clears. Whether a nap is possible at all is a roster and employer question, and worth asking.

practices.title: Coffee early in the shift, small after that
practices.summary: On nights, have the real coffee in the first hour or two of the shift; from about seven hours before your day sleep, keep it to one small cup.
practices.why: A randomised crossover with overnight recordings gave people a small or a large caffeine load at four, eight and twelve hours before bed. The small amount — about one cup — did not disturb sleep at any of those times; the large amount, about four cups’ worth, delayed sleep and broke it up even taken twelve hours out. So the rule is about size as much as clock time, and it is a generous one: you keep the coffee, you just front-load it. For an eight-thirty day sleep, that puts the big one before about one a.m. and anything after it small. Young men in one laboratory rather than shift workers, so a good rule to run on yourself.
practices.safety: Palpitations, reflux or anxiety around caffeine belong with a GP. Caffeine buys alertness on a night shift; it does not make the drive home safe.

practices.title: Point the light the right way after a long flight
practices.summary: Flying east: bright light in the morning after you arrive and none in the pre-dawn hours. Flying west: light in the evening, none early. Expect about an hour a day eastward and two westward; past eight zones east, shift the other way.
practices.why: The physiology is sound: laboratory studies mapped how a pulse of bright light moves the human clock earlier after the body’s temperature low point and later before it, and randomised pre-flight studies shifted people about an hour a day with timed morning light. What has not been shown is that the itineraries built from that physiology cut jet lag on a real trip — the one field review found most studies too small to tell. So this is the practice informed travellers use ahead of the evidence: the direction is right, the size of the win is yours to find out, and getting outside in the morning after an eastward flight costs nothing.
practices.safety: Past about eight zones the wrong direction can shift you the long way round; if you are unsure which way you are moving, keep your home schedule for a day rather than guess.

practices.title: Read your tracker for when, not how deep
practices.summary: Once a week, look at your watch or ring for the two things it does well — when you slept and roughly how long — and read the deep, light and REM minutes as a loose trend, never a verdict.
practices.why: Against laboratory sleep recording, consumer devices detect sleep well: more than nine in ten sleeping minutes are scored as sleep in every study of every generation, so timing and totals are trustworthy. Wake inside the night and the stages are where they guess — half or more of true wake is scored as sleep, and stage agreement runs from poor to moderate, which is why a bad night can look better on the screen than it felt. Used for timing, total and regularity across weeks, the tracker is genuinely useful; used to chase a deep-sleep number, it is a slot machine. Knowing which is which is what lets you keep enjoying it.
practices.safety: If checking the numbers is making you sleep worse, stop checking for a while — nothing is lost. A tracker cannot diagnose a sleep disorder; loud snoring, gasping, or daytime sleep attacks go to a doctor.

practices.title: Cold water on the days you don’t lift
practices.summary: If you love the plunge, keep it: put it on non-lifting days, or in the morning of an evening session, so it never lands in the hours after resistance training while muscle is the goal.
practices.why: This is the best-established finding in the cold literature and it is good news dressed as a caution — it tells you when to plunge, not whether. A twelve-week trial that iced one group after every lifting session found smaller gains in strength, muscle size and fibre growth than active recovery; a seven-week trial saw the fibre growth blunted; a leg-cooling study measured muscle-building about twelve percent lower over two weeks. Four pooled analyses through 2026 agree on the direction, with the size somewhere between small and moderate. Endurance training is fine either way: six weeks of sprint intervals with cold afterwards adapted just as well. Move the plunge to the morning or the rest day and you keep both the lift and the buzz.
practices.safety: The first thirty seconds bring a gasp and fast breathing that settle within two or three minutes: get in gradually, keep your head out, never hold your breath, and never plunge alone in open water. Minutes, not tens of minutes. A heart or rhythm condition, or pregnancy, means a doctor first. Educational structure, not medical advice.

practices.title: Ice bath after the week’s hardest session
practices.summary: After the hardest session of the week — the long run, the match, the brutal conditioning day — ten to fifteen minutes in water at ten to fifteen degrees, when being fresh tomorrow matters more than squeezing out the last adaptation.
practices.why: Cold water does one thing reliably: it takes the edge off soreness and helps next-day power. A Cochrane review of seventeen trials found less soreness at every point from one to four days after; a pooled analysis of fifty-two studies found modestly better next-day power after hard or eccentric work, with the best results around ten to fifteen degrees for ten to fifteen minutes. The trials are small and the reviewers say so, which is why this is a B and not an A. It is a trade rather than a free lunch — after ordinary lifting the same plunge blunts the adaptation — so spend it where it pays: the day you need to walk down stairs tomorrow.
practices.safety: In slowly, head out, no breath-holding, and out before your hands stop working. A heart or rhythm condition means not at all, and never alone. Dry layers and a hot drink afterwards — your temperature keeps dropping for a while after you climb out. Educational structure, not medical advice.

practices.title: The plunge after the sauna
practices.summary: If ending a sauna with cold water is your favourite part, keep it — briefly, feet first, head out — and enjoy it as a ritual, because that is what the evidence can honestly call it so far.
practices.why: This is the most popular pairing in the recovery world and nobody has yet tested it on any outcome. The nearest evidence is hot-and-cold water contrast for soreness, which beats sitting still and does not beat cold alone, and one study of eight winter swimmers who also used the sauna, which looked at how their bodies made heat and nothing about health. So the grade is the bottom one, and the ritual is still real: the jolt, the calm afterwards, the sleep that often follows a good evening in the heat. Some of that is the ritual itself, and the ritual works. Do it because you like it; that is a good enough reason.
practices.safety: Very hot to very cold asks the heart to do two opposite things at once. Never with a heart or rhythm condition, never after alcohol, never with the head under, and never straight from the hottest bench — sit a minute first. Out at the first dizziness. Educational structure, not medical advice.

practices.title: The strength floor: an hour a week
practices.summary: Whatever else the week holds, two short sessions of muscle-strengthening work — thirty to sixty minutes in total — and never a week at zero. Two twenty-minute sessions of bodyweight work at home count in full.
practices.why: Pooled cohort analyses find that people who do any muscle-strengthening work have meaningfully lower death rates over the following years than people who do none, on top of whatever aerobic activity they do. The best single piece of evidence follows a hundred and forty-seven thousand people for thirty years, and its shape is the encouraging part. Almost all of the benefit is already there by the first half hour a week, the curve stays flat across the next hour, and it bends back up beyond two hours. So there is a floor worth defending and no prize for piling on. This is association rather than proof, and strong people differ in many ways at once. If you already lift, this is the floor you never drop below on a bad week. If you do not, it is the smallest version that shows up in the data, and it is very small.
practices.safety: Technique before load, and build over months. A heart condition, joint or back trouble, or a long time away from training is a conversation with a doctor or physiotherapist before you start. Educational structure, not medical advice.

practices.title: The desk-day offset
practices.summary: On a day you sit for eight hours or more, bank thirty to forty minutes of brisk movement — walking counts, in pieces counts — and stand up out of every long stretch.
practices.why: Long sitting is associated with higher mortality in every large cohort, and the association mostly disappears in people who move enough. When activity was measured with worn devices across nine cohorts and forty-four thousand adults, about thirty to forty minutes a day of moderate-to-vigorous movement was where the sitting effect stopped showing — half the figure the earlier questionnaire studies had suggested, which is the good news here. Standing desks are not the same thing: a large device study found standing time unrelated to heart disease and, past two hours a day, linked to circulation trouble in the legs. Walk the long way to lunch, take the call on your feet, and the desk day is covered.
practices.safety: Brisk means breathing harder, not gasping. Chest pain, calf pain or unusual breathlessness while walking is a reason to see a doctor.

practices.title: Protein at every meal past sixty-five
practices.summary: Past sixty-five, put a proper serve of protein in each of three meals — the international PROT-AGE group describes a daily total around 1.0 to 1.2 grams per kilo of body weight — and pair it with the strength floor.
practices.why: Two expert groups, PROT-AGE and ESPEN, reached the same figure for healthy older adults, a quarter to a half above the general guideline, because ageing muscle responds less to each meal and needs a bigger nudge. That figure is consensus rather than a trial result, which is why the grade is a C. What is well established is the pairing: a meta-analysis of seventy-four randomised trials found extra protein adds lean mass when combined with resistance training, with the benefit in over-65s appearing between about 1.2 and 1.6 grams per kilo. Eggs at breakfast, something substantial at lunch, and the lifting twice a week: that is most of it, and it is very doable.
practices.safety: The figure is the position paper’s, for healthy adults: kidney or liver disease and several other conditions change what is appropriate, and a doctor or dietitian decides that. Any history of disordered eating means this card is one to work through with professional support rather than alone. Educational structure, not medical advice.

practices.title: Let the gap stretch
practices.summary: Once a week, push the things you now know solidly further out — daily to every few days, then to weekly. Keep the shaky ones close.
practices.why: Spacing your review beats cramming, and that part is settled. The useful question is how far apart, and there is an answer: across more than thirteen hundred people, the best gap scaled with how long you needed to remember something. Roughly a fifth to two fifths of the way out for something you need in a week, and a much smaller fraction of the distance for something you need in a year. In practice that means the gap should keep growing as an item gets solid, which is the opposite of reviewing everything equally. This works alongside your existing review rather than replacing it.

practices.title: Guess before you read
practices.summary: Before you open the chapter or the video, write three questions you think it will answer and your best guess at each. Then read. Being wrong is the point.
practices.why: Guessing before you learn something looks like a waste of the three minutes and is not. In a series of experiments, people who guessed first remembered more afterwards than people who simply studied for longer, and the gain showed up even on the questions they had guessed wrong. Something about having reached for an answer changes what happens when the real one arrives. The evidence is five experiments from one laboratory on one piece of reading, so this is worth trying rather than settled, and it costs three minutes at the front of something you were going to do anyway.
practices.safety: You are meant to get these wrong. A wrong guess is doing the work here, so do not tidy them up afterwards or grade yourself on them.

practices.title: One behaviour, one cue
practices.summary: Pick one small thing and one cue you meet every day. After the kettle goes on, or at seven, whichever you will actually notice. Then let it take the time it takes.
practices.why: A habit is a behaviour that has stopped costing a decision, and the research on how that happens is more forgiving than the folklore. It takes most people somewhere between two and four months, and the measured spread runs from about three weeks to most of a year, so any single number you have been given is somebody rounding. The cue can be a routine or a clock time; a trial that compared them directly found no difference, so use whichever you will notice. And the finding that matters most on a bad week: missing one day did not measurably set people back.

practices.title: Sleep is the second half of the session
practices.summary: Sunday, five minutes: put the hardest new physical practice on a day you will sleep normally afterwards. Not the night before an early start.
practices.why: When you learn something with your hands — an instrument, a lift, a language's sounds, a craft — a good deal of the consolidation happens while you sleep. Pooled across dozens of studies with more than sixteen hundred people, groups who slept after practising outperformed groups who stayed awake by a moderate margin. The studies used simple laboratory tasks rather than a guitar, and nobody has tested the scheduling instruction itself, which is why this is a planning nudge rather than a promise. It costs nothing to put the hard session on a night you will sleep properly.

practices.title: Learn the ground before the technique
practices.summary: Starting something new: spend one session just getting the map. The names, the shape, the vocabulary. Before any book on how to study it.
practices.why: Study technique cannot compensate for not knowing what the passage is about. In the study that made this vivid, children who were weak readers but knew the game outperformed strong readers who did not, on every measure, and knowing the subject helped regardless of reading ability. That is one small study from the 1980s in one domain, so treat it as a good prior rather than a finding. It matches what most people notice anyway: the second book in a field is far easier than the first, and it is not because your technique improved.

practices.title: Finish on one you got right
practices.summary: When the session is nearly done, do one repetition you know you can do well. Then stop there.
practices.why: This is a craftsman's habit rather than a finding, and it is worth saying so plainly. The idea that the last repetition gets consolidated preferentially overnight is not something anyone has shown, and we looked. What is true is smaller and still good: ending on something that went well is a better place to stop, it makes the next session easier to walk into, and walking in is most of the battle. Some of this is the ritual itself, and the ritual works.

practices.title: The week that collapsed
practices.summary: When the week falls apart: one hard set each of a squat, a press and a pull, twice or three times. Fifteen minutes. That is the whole session.
practices.why: A review that went looking for the least training that still builds strength found that a single hard set per exercise, done a couple of times a week, produces real gains. The authors' own phrase for it is "suboptimal, yet significant", and that is exactly the right framing: this is not your best week and it still counts. Be aware the review is small, six studies, no control groups and men only, so treat the size of the gain as roughly right rather than precise. What is not in doubt is the direction. Fifteen minutes beats the zero you were considering.
practices.safety: Close to failure is not grinding. Stop the set when your form changes, not when the rep fails. Two lighter ramping sets first, because one working set does not mean a cold one. Never push through joint pain. Educational structure, not medical advice.

practices.title: Steady on your feet
practices.summary: Past sixty-five: two or three sessions a week that mix balance work with resistance work, kept up for at least three months.
practices.why: This is the best-evidenced thing in the whole training pillar and almost nobody talks about it. A network analysis of two hundred and nineteen randomised trials covering a hundred and sixty-seven thousand people found that balance and resistance work together is what prevents falls. Three things in it make this warmer than it sounds. It was the format participants preferred over the alternatives. Doing it alone rather than in a group was also preferred, with high confidence, so home is the version people actually want. And adding more components did not add benefit, which means nobody needs a programme. The honest caveat is that the trials were supervised and ran longer than three months, so this is the unsupervised approximation of a supervised thing.
practices.safety: Something solid within reach for every set — a bench, a worktop, a door frame. No eyes-closed balance work unless somebody is with you. If you have fallen in the last year, feel dizzy on standing, or take medication that affects balance, start this with a doctor or physiotherapist rather than alone; the trials behind it were supervised and people at real risk should be too. Educational structure, not medical advice.

practices.title: Three short hard bursts
practices.summary: If you do no formal exercise at all: three to five bursts of about a minute, hard, spread through the day. Stairs, a hill, anything that makes talking difficult.
practices.why: For someone doing nothing, the gap between nothing and a little is the biggest gap there is, and it does not require a gym or a change of clothes. Short vigorous bursts scattered through an ordinary day improve fitness in randomised trials, and very large activity-tracker studies find that brief bursts occurring naturally in daily life track lower mortality. This is explicitly the card for people who are not going to start training, and the bursts have to be genuinely hard for about a minute. Walking to the shops does not count; walking up the hill to the shops fast does.
practices.safety: Hard means hard for you: breathing too heavily to hold a conversation, not flat out. If you have a heart condition, chest pain on exertion, or have been inactive for years, talk to a doctor before adding vigorous bursts. Stop for chest pain, unusual breathlessness or dizziness and get it looked at. Educational structure, not medical advice.

practices.title: You have one more than you think
practices.summary: On the last set of a lift you know well: when you feel you have two reps left, you probably have three. Do one of them.
practices.why: People are reliably conservative about how close they are to failure, and the size of the error has been measured: about one repetition, in the same direction almost every time. That matters because most of what makes a set productive happens in the last few hard repetitions, so a consistent one-rep underestimate means quietly training a bit easier than you think you are. This is a calibration nudge rather than an instruction to grind, and it applies to the last set of a movement you are confident in, not to a new lift or a heavy single.
practices.safety: Only on a lift you know well, with the bar in a position you can safely fail or rack. Not on a heavy single, not on a new movement, and not when you are alone under a loaded bar without safety pins. Form changing is the signal to stop regardless of how many reps you think are left. Educational structure, not medical advice.

practices.title: Leave two in the tank
practices.summary: If what you want is to be stronger rather than bigger, stop each set about two repetitions short. You do not have to go to failure.
practices.why: Training to the point where the next repetition is impossible feels like the serious option and mostly is not. When proximity to failure was compared directly, strength gains were similar whether people stopped a couple of reps short or went all the way, while going to failure cost more fatigue and made the next session worse. Size is a slightly different question and does respond to pushing closer. So if strength is the goal, stopping short is not the soft version, it is the version that lets you do the next session properly.
practices.safety: Leaving repetitions is the conservative choice and needs no caution of its own. The usual applies: warm up, stop when form changes, and do not train through joint pain. Educational structure, not medical advice.

practices.title: Move one lift fast
practices.summary: Past sixty: on one exercise a session, drive the lifting phase as fast as you can while keeping the lowering slow and controlled.
practices.why: Strength and power are not the same thing, and power fades earlier. Power is what catches you when you trip and what gets you out of a low chair, so it is worth training on purpose rather than hoping it comes along with everything else. The way to train it is not heavier, it is faster: same weight, intent to move it quickly on the way up. The trials here are smaller than the falls-prevention evidence and one of them overstates its own non-significant results, so treat this as a sensible addition to work you are already doing rather than a replacement for it.
practices.safety: Fast on the way up, controlled on the way down, and never a rushed or bouncing descent, which is where people get hurt. Not on a maximal load. If you have joint replacements, osteoporosis, or a history of back or shoulder injury, run this past a physiotherapist first. Educational structure, not medical advice.

practices.title: Slow and heavy, through the full range
practices.summary: Once or twice a week, include one exercise done slowly and heavily through a long range. Tendons adapt to load, and they need a different kind of it.
practices.why: Tendons are slower to adapt than muscle, and the thing they adapt to is high strain rather than high volume or high speed. That is why the achy tendon usually shows up when training has been going well: the muscle got stronger faster than the tissue attaching it. Slow heavy work through a long range is what the evidence points at. It is not a treatment for a painful tendon, which is a different problem needing a different plan, and the studies here are modest, so this is a sensible inclusion rather than a guarantee.
practices.safety: This is for healthy tendons. A tendon that is already painful, swollen, or worse the morning after is a physiotherapist conversation, not a heavier session. Build the load over weeks rather than sessions, because tendons adapt more slowly than the muscles pulling on them. Educational structure, not medical advice.

practices.title: Ride rather than run on cardio days
practices.summary: If you are lifting for strength and also doing cardio, put the cardio on a bike rather than a run where you can, and not right before legs.
practices.why: Doing endurance work alongside lifting costs a little of the strength and size you would otherwise get, and the size of that cost depends on what kind of cardio and when. Running appears to cost more than cycling, plausibly because of the eccentric loading, and the interference is smaller when the two are further apart in the day or the week. The effect is modest and the evidence is a set of small studies rather than anything definitive, so this is a preference rather than a rule, and doing the cardio you will actually do beats optimising which kind.
practices.safety: Nothing here asks anyone to train harder, so the only caution is the ordinary one: if cardio is new to you and you have a heart condition or risk factors, start it with a doctor. Educational structure, not medical advice.

practices.title: Move first, decide later
practices.summary: On the days work was heaviest, go straight into twenty minutes of moving before you sit down. Walking counts. Ten minutes counts.
practices.why: There is a good reason the session gets skipped after a hard day, and it is not the one everybody assumes. A diary study following employees across hundreds of days found the thing that predicted skipping was not being physically tired. It was still being mentally at work. So the decision is the hard part, not the exercise, which is why this card asks you to start moving before you decide anything. Movement is one of the few off-work activities that shows up consistently in the recovery research, and the version that works is the one you chose.
practices.safety: On a night rotation this competes with sleep, and sleep wins. After a run of nights, take the sleep and move after it rather than before.

practices.title: Protect the days off you actually have
practices.summary: One block on each stretch of days off: something with people in it, and the errands kept out of it. Whatever day of the week that lands on.
practices.why: A study of eighty-seven emergency service workers followed them across their days off and found what predicted coming back worse rather than better. Not the work. It was the days off filling with hassles, and the absence of people in them. Two things follow. Time off is not automatically recovery, and the calendar version of a weekend is irrelevant if yours falls on a Tuesday. This card exists because most advice about weekends quietly assumes you get Saturday.

practices.title: The holiday works, and it fades
practices.summary: Before a break: write the one thing about work you want to be different when you get back. The rest of the lift is not meant to last.
practices.why: Pooled holiday studies find a real improvement in wellbeing during the break and a return close to baseline soon after going back. Both halves are normal. Knowing the second half in advance is worth something, because the alternative is reading an ordinary fade as evidence you wasted the leave or that something is wrong with you. Nothing is. A holiday is a rest, not a repair, and if you come back to the same job you come back to the same job. That is what the one thing is for.

practices.title: This one is not yours to fix alone
practices.summary: If you are burnt out: name which part of the job is doing it, and who has the authority to change it. That sentence is the work. Not another evening practice.
practices.why: This is the clearest finding in the whole pillar and it does not flatter an app. Across pooled controlled trials, changes to the job move burnout roughly two and a half times as far as anything aimed at the individual. In workers who already meet the threshold, the pooled individual trials show no effect on exhaustion or cynicism at all. So the honest thing to say is that a breathing practice is not the treatment for an unsustainable role, and being unable to fix it on your own is not a shortfall in you. What does help is getting specific about which part of it is wrong, because that is the thing that can be raised, and vague exhaustion cannot be.
practices.safety: Burnout and depression overlap and this card cannot tell them apart. If the flatness is there on days off too, or you are not safe, that is a GP conversation rather than a work one. Lifeline is 13 11 14.

practices.title: Steer it back to the work
practices.summary: When feedback arrives, ask one question about the thing itself: what would have made it better? If the conversation turns to what you are like, turn it back.
practices.why: The largest analysis of feedback ever assembled, over six hundred effects, found something nobody expects: more than a third of feedback interventions made performance worse. The mechanism is the useful part. Feedback helps when attention lands on the task and hurts when it lands on the self, because a person defending their character has stopped thinking about the work. You cannot control how it is delivered. You can control which of those two things you ask about, and one question is usually enough to move it.

practices.title: A rating is mostly about the rater
practices.summary: After a review that stung: write what was actually about the work, and what was about the person writing it. Act on the first list.
practices.why: When researchers decomposed thousands of performance ratings to see what they were actually measuring, the largest share by far was the individual quirks of whoever was doing the rating. The share attributable to the performance being rated was roughly a fifth. That is not a reason to dismiss feedback, and the first list on this card is the real one. It is a reason not to reorganise your sense of yourself around one number from one person, which is what a bad review invites you to do on the day you get it.

practices.title: Change one thing about the job itself
practices.summary: Monthly, two columns: one change that helps the work, one change that helps you. Pick one from each and do them this month.
practices.why: Reshaping your own role, the tasks, the framing, who you do them with, has been tested as an intervention rather than just described, and it raises engagement reliably. The detail that matters is why this card has two columns. The trials that worked asked people to plan for the organisation and for themselves together; the versions covering only one side did much less. So it is not a card about making work nicer. It is a card about making a change you can defend to the person who approves it.

practices.title: Add the harder thing, not just remove the annoying one
practices.summary: Once a quarter, name one genuinely harder piece of work to take on. Ask for it. Do not wait to be offered it.
practices.why: When the parts of job crafting were separated out and tested against how other people rated the work, one part carried almost all of the performance link: taking on more challenging demands. Cutting the annoying parts, which is the version most people mean by the phrase, performed weakest and did not even group statistically with the others. That is a genuinely useful asymmetry. Reducing the irritating bits of a job makes it less irritating. Adding a harder bit is the one that shows up in what other people see.

practices.title: Count the gaps under eleven hours
practices.summary: When next week’s roster lands, mark every gap between shifts shorter than eleven hours. Write the number down. That number is the thing to raise.
practices.why: The short turnaround between two shifts has a name in the research and a threshold attached to it, and eleven hours is the figure both a large registry study and a hospital trial used. Fewer of them means less sleep lost and less fatigue on shift. The trial is also honest about size: halving them bought a real but modest improvement, not a transformation. You mostly cannot change your own roster, which is exactly why this card is about counting rather than fixing. Turning up to a roster conversation with a number is a different conversation from turning up tired.
practices.safety: Fatigue is a hazard your employer has a legal duty to manage, not a personal weakness. Break entitlements come from your award or agreement rather than from the Act, so read yours before the conversation.

practices.title: The drive home is the last shift
practices.summary: Before a run of nights starts, arrange how you get home after the last one. A lift, a nap first, a different way. Decide it now, not at seven in the morning.
practices.why: Driving after a night shift is measurably dangerous, and the reason this card fires days early is that the moment you need the decision is the worst possible moment to make it. At the end of the last night you are impaired, you want to be home, and the arrangement is no longer arrangeable. Four days earlier it costs one message. This is the arrangement; the app already carries the card about not driving, and they are meant to work together.
practices.safety: If you are already at the end of the run with nothing arranged, sleep before driving rather than pushing through. A nap in the car park is not a failure, it is the correct answer.

practices.title: Three words for the roster conversation
practices.summary: Before any roster or agreement discussion, take three things that have evidence behind them: forward rotation, faster rotation, and a say in your own shifts.
practices.why: Most of what gets argued about in roster consultations has nothing behind it. Three things do. Rotating forwards rather than backwards, rotating quickly rather than slowly, and letting people have some say in their own shifts all show up in the review evidence as better for sleep and health. That is a short list and it is worth knowing precisely because it is short. Going in with three specific asks that a manager can look up is a different position from going in with a complaint.
practices.safety: None of this is a promise the answer will be yes, and a roster you cannot change is not a personal failure. Everything an individual can do sits at the bottom of the safety hierarchy; the design of the roster sits near the top, and that is the employer’s job.

practices.title: A start time, a finish time, and one thing outside
practices.summary: While you are between jobs: a fixed time you start, a fixed time you stop, and one reason to leave the house. Every weekday.
practices.why: When researchers pooled hundreds of studies on what protects wellbeing during unemployment, the strongest things were not about the job search at all. They were having a structure to the day, keeping contact with people, and having ways of coping. The applications matter for getting work. The shape of the day is what keeps you well enough to keep making them. This is the best-evidenced card in the round and it asks nothing about your search.
practices.safety: Job loss is a genuine loss and it is normal for this to be hard. If the low mood is not lifting, your GP is the right door, and Lifeline is 13 11 14.

practices.title: Practise it out loud, with someone
practices.summary: One block a week: say your answers out loud to an actual person, and have them push back. Not another hour of applications.
practices.why: The pooled trials of job-search programmes give an unusually specific instruction. Programmes that taught the skills alone did not work. Programmes that offered encouragement alone did not work. Programmes that did both roughly tripled the odds of finding work. Practising out loud with someone who will push back is the cheapest thing that contains both halves, because it is a skill rehearsal and it is another person in your corner on the same afternoon.

practices.title: Write the knockbacks before they arrive
practices.summary: Once at the start, then monthly: write the three knockbacks you expect, and one line each on what you will do the day after.
practices.why: A large randomised job-search trial built this in deliberately and named it as one of the active parts: telling people the setbacks were coming and having them plan for them in advance. It works for the same reason if-then plans work generally, which the app already uses elsewhere. A rejection you planned for is an event. A rejection you did not is a verdict. Writing them down beforehand does not make them pleasant, it makes them survivable on the day.

practices.title: Write down the doors in week one
practices.summary: Once, early: write down which government and support services exist for your situation, before you need them and before it feels urgent.
practices.why: Australia has income support, career transition help for people over forty-five, and separate programmes for younger workers and for parents. None of it is hard to find and all of it is harder to face in week six than in week one, when it is still an administrative task rather than an admission. This card is a list, not advice, and it exists because the cost of writing it down early is ten minutes and the cost of not having it later is much higher.
practices.safety: What you are eligible for and what any of it pays are questions for Services Australia, not for this app. If money is the immediate problem, the National Debt Helpline on 1800 007 007 is free and its financial counsellors sell nothing.

practices.title: Start it at the minute it says
practices.summary: Any meeting you run starts on time, even with people missing. Especially with people missing.
practices.why: A field study measured what a late start actually costs and the answer was not just goodwill. Meetings that began around ten minutes late produced ideas that were rated worse in quality and less workable, not merely fewer of them. That makes starting on time the best-supported meeting practice there is and also the only free one. Everything else on the list costs preparation. This costs a decision you make once and then hold.

practices.title: Stand up for the short ones
practices.summary: For a quick status meeting, take the chairs away. Expect it to be shorter, not better.
practices.why: When sitting and standing meetings were compared directly, the sitting ones ran about a third longer and produced decisions of the same quality. That is a real saving and it is worth being precise about what it buys. In the same study the standing groups were slightly less satisfied and used slightly less of the information they had. So this is a card about reclaiming minutes from a status update, not a better way to make a decision, and it should never be used for the meeting where something difficult gets worked out.

practices.title: Say that cameras off is fine
practices.summary: On a heavy day of calls, say out loud that cameras are optional. If you run the meeting, you are the one who can.
practices.why: A field experiment that actually manipulated the camera found that keeping it on across a day of calls left people more tired, and that the tiredness showed up in how much they spoke and engaged. The effect was larger for women and for newer staff, which is the part that turns this from a personal tip into something a person running the meeting should say. Someone junior asking to turn their camera off is taking a risk. Someone senior saying it is fine here removes the risk for everybody at once.

practices.title: Ten minutes after the bad one
practices.summary: After a meeting that went badly, book ten minutes before the next thing. Not to fix it. To stop carrying it into the next hour.
practices.why: The cost of a bad meeting does not stop when the meeting does, and survey work on this finds the need to recover afterwards tracks how poor and how irrelevant the meeting felt. What that costs in minutes is not established, and the confident figure that circulates does not trace to anything, so this card does not give you one. What it gives you is the shape: the next hour is where the damage actually lands, and ten booked minutes is a cheap way to keep it out.

practices.title: Build into the heat over a week
practices.summary: First hot week of the season: build up exposure over several days, plan where the shade and the breaks are, and learn the early warning signs.
practices.why: Working in heat measurably raises the risk of injury and of losing productivity, and the body does adapt, but it adapts over about a week rather than in a day. Planning that week deliberately is the difference between adapting and being caught out on the first thirty-eight degree day. The cheap controls are the ones with the evidence: building up gradually, planned breaks in shade, and knowing what the early signs feel like before they become an emergency.
practices.safety: Rescheduling or stopping work in extreme heat is the first control in the Australian hierarchy, not the last, and it is the employer’s call to make available. Confusion, stopping sweating, or collapse are emergencies: call 000. If you take medication that affects sweating or fluid balance, ask your pharmacist before a hot run of days.

practices.title: Take the break for the right reason
practices.summary: Take the break because it makes the afternoon feel better. Take a longer one after heavy work. Do not take it to get more done.
practices.why: Pooled trials of short work breaks found a clear improvement in how energetic and how tired people felt, and no reliable improvement in how much they produced, except on the easiest tasks. That is worth knowing rather than hiding, because the productivity promise is the thing that makes people feel guilty about breaks and then skip them. Feeling better through the afternoon is a good enough reason on its own. The other finding is practical: after genuinely heavy work, ten minutes was not enough, and longer breaks did more.

practices.title: Stop building the feedback sandwich
practices.summary: You can stop wrapping criticism in praise. Say the thing about the work, plainly and kindly, and keep every sentence about the work.
practices.why: The whole empirical literature on the praise-criticism-praise structure is about three studies. One found it changed what people thought of the feedback and not what they did with it. Another found a benefit in ninety-one students where the authors could not tell whether it came from the structure or simply from there being something positive in the message at all. Meanwhile the big feedback analysis shows that feedback fails when attention moves from the task to the person, and wrapping a criticism in unrelated praise is a technique for making a conversation more about the person. The alternative is not bluntness. It is staying on the work.

practices.title: Write alone first, then pool
practices.summary: Before any idea meeting, everyone writes alone for five minutes. Then pool. Skip the open round-the-table brainstorm.
practices.why: Groups brainstorming out loud reliably produce fewer and worse ideas than the same people working alone and combining afterwards. That has held up across decades of studies, and the pattern inside it is immediately usable: the loss gets bigger with bigger groups, bigger when someone is watching, and bigger when people speak rather than write. So the fix is not a better facilitator. It is five quiet minutes with a pen before anybody talks, which costs nothing and is the version that tests better.

practices.title: Stop worrying about multitasking either way
practices.summary: You cannot train yourself to multitask, and you have not damaged your brain by trying. Keep the one thing that does hold: switching costs, so batch the switches.
practices.why: Two beliefs circulate here and neither survives. There is no good evidence that multitasking improves with practice. There is also no solid evidence for the frightening half, that heavy multitaskers have worse attention: the original finding did not replicate cleanly and the pooled association went away once small-study effects were corrected for. What does hold is that switching between tasks costs something each time, which the app already covers. That is the whole of it, and it means the guilt was doing no work.

practices.title: The personality test is not a team plan
practices.summary: You can skip building a team around type letters. Keep the conversation the workshop started, and drop the instrument.
practices.why: The popular workplace type instruments give unstable results on retest and there is no body of evidence that a type predicts how someone performs or how a team does. That is not the same as saying the day was worthless. Getting a team to talk openly about how each of them prefers to work is genuinely useful, and it is the conversation doing that, not the letters. Keep the conversation, have it for free, and spend the budget on something with evidence behind it.

practices.title: Open plan did not make you talk more
practices.summary: If the open office is not producing the collaboration it promised, that is the normal result. Book the conversation you need rather than waiting to bump into it.
practices.why: Two companies were measured with wearable sensors and message logs before and after moving to open plan, which is a much better test than asking people how they feel about it. Face-to-face interaction fell by around seventy percent, and electronic messaging rose to replace it. People appear to withdraw when they lose the ability to control who can see and hear them. So the collaboration the layout promised does not arrive by proximity, and waiting to bump into someone is not a plan. Ask for the ten minutes.

practices.title: Tonight, in your own words
practices.summary: Early in the evening, one written line for tonight — “when X happens, I do Y” — naming the moment you expect and the thing you will actually do.
practices.why: Naming the exact cue and the exact response ahead of time is the best-replicated finding in behaviour change: about ninety-four studies pooled to a medium-to-large effect. Inside those studies the plans that worked best were contingent — an if and a then — were made by people who wanted the goal, and had been rehearsed at least once. Writing tonight’s line is that rehearsal. Two details carry the weight: the cue must be a real moment (the sofa at nine, the fourth round at the same table), and the then must be something you do, because a plan written as “I will not” leaves nothing to do with the moment. Graded B rather than A because the daily, one-night form is a moderator inside those trials rather than a trial of its own; the weekly three-moment plan in this library holds the A.
practices.safety: Support for a habit you can safely change on your own, and nothing more. Daily use, shakes, sweating, a racing heart or bad anxiety without it, or not being able to stop once started, is a doctor’s call — and stopping suddenly after heavy daily drinking can be dangerous. Free, confidential helplines exist in most countries for drinking, drugs and gambling; a doctor or pharmacist can name the one where you live. IntentNorth never charges for any of this.

practices.title: A stand-in that fits the trigger
practices.summary: When the urge lands, do the one thing you chose for this trigger for one to three minutes — long breaths out for stress, something for your hands when bored, your drink, your line and your exit decided before a social night, the smallest thing and bed when tired.
practices.why: Habit reversal training — notice the cue, then perform a competing action that cannot happen at the same time as the habit, held for a minute or three — is the best-supported approach for repetitive habits like nail biting and hair pulling, and matching the action to the cue is part of the method rather than a flourish. The matching is what the evidence on triggers supports: a stress urge is arousal looking for an exit and falls to a long exhale; boredom wants stimulation, not sedation; a social urge is decided before arriving, because the refusal that works is the one rehearsed; a tired evening cannot carry a big answer, so it gets a small one. Graded C because the trials are in body-focused habits, and carrying the method to drinking, vaping and scrolling is a reasonable extension rather than a tested one.

practices.title: Ten minutes first
practices.summary: Before acting on the urge, ten minutes and one change of place — the phone in another room, a glass of water, a different chair — and then decide.
practices.why: A pause between the pull and the act is the one in-the-moment phone finding with real numbers behind it. When a short wait and a question were put in front of a chosen app, people abandoned about a third of the opens they had started and tried to open it about a third less often, across tens of thousands of uses. The wait is not the point; deciding after it is, because the decision the habit was making for you gets made by you. The ten minutes is a rule of thumb, and the phone data is a field study rather than a randomised trial, so C. What it does not do is make the urge go away — it puts a gap where the habit had none.

practices.title: After a slip, the next hour
practices.summary: When it has already happened: water, a different room, the stand-in you chose, and bed at the usual time. The next hour is the whole plan, and nothing restarts from zero.
practices.why: One slip rarely does the damage on its own. What predicts the slide is the account given of it — that the run is dead, that this proves something permanent, so the rest of the night may as well go the same way. In the smoking relapse work the guilt after a first lapse did not predict relapse; the drop in confidence after later ones did, and putting the blame on the setup rather than the self protected against the next one. So the hour after a slip is where the story gets written, and a short, specific hour writes a short story: one event, one fixable cause, the ordinary night resumed. Graded C because the evidence is observational and about interpretation, not a trial of the hour itself. Counters that reset to zero hand the story its ending, which is why IntentNorth counts wins and never resets anything.
